This presumption is based above all on the high probability that a child born during marriage will have blood ties with the husband under the social background that a wife in a marriage is naturally expected to conceive the husband’s child.
However, with the recent rapid development of medical technology concerning assisted reproduction, including artificial insemination, the social and cultural background underlying the Civil Act provisions on natural children has itself changed in family law, and ethical issues and legal tasks that cannot be resolved by existing Civil Act provisions and traditional doctrine have newly arisen. Representative examples include the fact that persons who previously could not have children due to infertility or sterility are now able to become parents with the help of assisted reproductive technology, and how to regulate the parent-child relationship of a child born through such technology. What was once a “problem of fate” has today become a “problem of choice,” and public discussion of the ethical and social responsibility is urgently needed. Due to the development of genetic testing technology, uncertainty of blood ties in the father-child relationship, which is the premise for applying the presumption, can no longer exist. As the majority opinion does, it should not be said that a separate legal requirement such as presumption or acknowledgment is necessary for the father-child relationship unlike the mother-child relationship. It is now time to seriously discuss the legal evaluation of the intent of husband and wife who wished to have a child through artificial insemination and the limits of their responsibility.
(2) As a principle, legal regulation of newly arising social phenomena should be made through legislation, that is, enactment or amendment of statutes. However, even though legal disputes arising from a new social phenomenon are actually occurring, if legislation of the law to be applied in adjudication has not yet been enacted, the courts vested with judicial power by the Constitution cannot refuse to adjudicate. Therefore, courts must discover and declare the legal principles that a reasonable legislator would naturally have taken as a standard norm in such situations. Such judge-made law is properly included in judicial power as an effort to bridge the gap between social reality and the legal order when a vacuum in law arises due to the legislature’s failure to exercise its legislative power despite changing social reality. This judicial process of identifying law is distinct from analogical application or analogical interpretation of statutes. Analogical application means applying legal norms concerning a similar matter, to the extent justified in light of the legal system, legislative intent and purpose, to matters for which there is a gap in regulation the legislature did not intend despite legislation; see Justice Kim Jae-hyeong’s concurrence in 2012다74236. Even only for the birth of an artificial insemination child through assisted reproduction, there are various types, including not only cases like this one where sperm donation using a third party’s sperm is performed, but also cases where an egg from a third party other than the wife is provided or a child is born through surrogate arrangement. Whether such matters should be permitted from the standpoint of the legal order as a whole, and if so how the establishment of parent-child relationship should be regulated from the standpoint of family law, are matters to be resolved by legislation, not by applying existing presumption provisions as the majority opinion argues. Courts must exercise judicial power by going through the process of forming the most appropriate dispute-resolution standard for resolving the matter at hand, that is, concrete and historical law, by comprehensively considering the constitutional provisions relating thereto and their relationship with other statutes, the fundamental values pursued by the law, and the generally shared legal consciousness of society.
Comparatively speaking, many legal systems have resolved this issue by separately enacting legislation. In Korea too, although legislative efforts have been made several times, they have not borne fruit. As the majority opinion also points out, at the time of the Civil Act enactment in 1958, it could not be envisaged that a wife could conceive and give birth to a child through artificial insemination, and therefore there was of course no need for a provision on this matter.
(3) The parent-child relationship between parents and children, together with the marital relationship, belongs to the most fundamental and private sphere of human life and at the same time becomes the basis of family relations under the Civil Act as the foundation for forming our community. The Constitution declares in Article 10 that all citizens shall be assured of human dignity and the right to pursue happiness, in Article 17 that all citizens shall not be infringed upon in their privacy, and in Article 36(1) that marriage and family life shall be established and maintained on the basis of individual dignity and equality of the sexes, and the State shall guarantee this. Therefore, parents’ efforts to have children constitute exercise of the right to pursue happiness and of the autonomous decision-making right concerning formation of family relations, and must be respected to the fullest extent unless they infringe another person’s fundamental rights or the public interest; secrecy must also be guaranteed.
The Civil Act provides procedures such as disavowal or action for confirmation so that parent-child relationship and true blood relationship may be aligned on the premise that natural parent-child relationships between parents and children require blood relationship. Nevertheless, where the child’s welfare and prompt determination of the parent-child relationship is deemed to take precedence, it prevents arbitrary denial of an already formed parent-child relationship from a social perspective. The limitations such as standing and filing period on the action for disavowal are examples. In this way, the Civil Act normatively first forms a family relationship called parent-child relationship on the basis of the fact that the child was born in a marital relationship and grants strong legal protection to that relationship; as the majority opinion points out, this is a legislative decision left to the legislature’s discretion and should be understood as reflecting the fundamental values pursued by the law and the generally shared legal consciousness of society. Such values pursued by the Civil Act regulating family relations, and the legal sentiment or legal consciousness generally discernible therefrom, should also be respected in setting the standard for the establishment of the parent-child relationship of an artificial insemination child.
If husband and wife, in the course of the artificial insemination child’s birth, consented to assisted reproductive procedure through true concurrence of intent, this means that, both privately and socially, they assume parental responsibility for the child with the intent of becoming the child’s parents. At this point, the husband is not merely consenting to the wife’s artificial insemination procedure. It is more consistent with reality to understand that the husband participates in the procedure from an equal position with the wife, by the unified intent of the spouses, and thereby actualizes the intent to establish a parent-child relationship with the child born therefrom.
As discussed above, where a husband and wife who are in a marriage have a concurrence of intent regarding the birth of an artificial insemination child and, on that basis, consent to the assisted reproductive procedure of artificial insemination using a third party’s sperm, the child should be regarded as the spouses’ natural child. This best accords with the Constitution’s principles of the people’s right to pursue happiness, the secrecy and freedom of private life, and the guarantee of family life; harmonizes with the Civil Act provisions concerning family relations; and accords with the basic values pursued by law as well as society’s generally shared legal sentiment and consciousness. Furthermore, the husband and wife’s concurrence of intent and consent to the procedure cannot be reversed retroactively, because doing so would contravene the constitutional decision on human dignity and value, the basic order of the Civil Act concerning parent-child relationships, and good morals and social order.
(4) The lower court did not accept the Plaintiff’s appeal against the first-instance judgment dismissing this part of the action, and gave the following reasons. The non-party, with the consent of the Plaintiff who was the spouse, received sperm from a third party and conceived and gave birth to Defendant 1 through artificial insemination, and therefore Defendant 1 is presumed to be the Plaintiff’s natural child under Article 844(1). It is unlawful for the Plaintiff to seek, against Defendant 1 who is subject to the presumption of paternity, confirmation of the nonexistence of the natural parent-child relationship by an action under Article 865.
As described in detail by the majority opinion, according to the factual circumstances discernible from the lower court judgment and the record, it can be seen that the Plaintiff agreed with the non-party, his then wife, with the intent to establish a parent-child relationship with Defendant 1, and that Defendant 1 was born through artificial insemination on that basis. Therefore, Defendant 1 constitutes the Plaintiff’s natural child, and the action for confirmation of nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship filed by the Plaintiff against Defendant 1 should be dismissed as without merit. However, in this case where only the Plaintiff has appealed, under the principle prohibiting reformatio in peius, the Court cannot render a judgment more unfavorable to the Plaintiff than the lower court’s judgment deeming this part of the action unlawful and dismissing it. Ultimately, the Plaintiff’s appeal as to Defendant 1 is dismissed.
B. As to the grounds for appeal concerning Defendant 2
(1) Under existing Supreme Court precedents, as to the scope of application of the presumption of paternity provision, the Supreme Court in the en banc judgment 82므59 stated that Article 844 applies where the spouses are cohabiting and in a state where the wife can conceive a child of the husband, and where there are outwardly apparent circumstances making it impossible for the wife to conceive a child of the husband due to lack of cohabitation, such as where one spouse has been abroad for a long period or the spouses are separated due to de facto divorce, the presumption does not apply. Since then, through a number of decisions, the Court has consistently maintained the position of recognizing exceptions to the presumption under certain requirements; see 87므73, 88므85, 91므566, 99므1817, 2000므292.
In the present case, however, the majority opinion says that even if it is revealed that a child conceived and born by the wife during marriage has no blood relationship with the husband, the presumption still applies, and gives detailed reasons. Examining those reasons, first, determining the scope based on blood relationship is contrary to the text and effectively renders the provision dead letter; second, if the scope of effect is determined based on blood relationship, a third party not in the family relation inevitably becomes deeply involved in private areas inside the home; and third, blood relationship may be a ground for rebutting the presumption, but cannot be a ground for determining the scope in which the presumption does not apply.
Considering the majority opinion in light of its reasons, it may appear to suggest changing the existing limitation theory by holding that no exception may be recognized even where absence of blood relationship is confirmed. On the other hand, it may also be read as maintaining the precedents by not expressing a view on this issue on the ground that this case is not one to which the precedents on exceptions apply. Although unnecessary legal confusion should be avoided, the majority opinion is not clear. Accordingly, while we agree that the presumption cannot be said not to apply merely because it has been revealed that the child has no blood relationship with the husband, we wish to state our separate opinion regarding whether there should be limits on the scope of application and the standards for such determination.
(2) The above en banc judgment in 82므59 changed the prior unlimited theory to the limitation theory, stating that Article 844 together with the disavowal provisions was established for the peace of the family on the premise that the spouses are carrying on normal married life, and that applying it even where that premise is not satisfied and causing the matter to be resolved by the strict disavowal action would run counter to the purpose of the system and may produce unjust results, such as promoting the establishment of father-child relationships contrary to true blood relations. This was an effort, under the historical background when scientific proof of blood ties was difficult and the old Civil Act limited standing to the husband and filing period to 1 year, to harmoniously interpret the legal interest of domestic peace and the principle of truth in blood relationships. The Constitutional Court also understands the issue of the scope of application as a matter of how to harmonize the interests of the mother, child, biological father, and father in aligning the legal parent-child relationship with truth and the interest in legal stability through prompt determination. Thus the matter is in principle left to the legislature’s discretion; however, if the standard is excessively unreasonable or the means of escape are excessively limited so that it compels a parent-child relationship contrary to true blood relationship, then it exceeds the limits of legislative formation and is unconstitutional; see Constitutional Court en banc decision 2013헌마623.
However, compared with 1983 when the above en banc judgment first recognized an exception, today’s circumstances have greatly changed in social, technological, and legal respects, so the precedents that adopt the outward appearance theory as the criterion for exception need to be comprehensively reconsidered.
First, divorce and remarriage have increased sharply, and social perceptions of divorce and remarriage have also changed significantly. Accordingly, relevant laws and institutions have changed, and the Civil Act provision that prohibited remarriage of women for a certain period was abolished, while the period from breakdown of the marital relationship to the effectuation of divorce has become longer, increasing the possibility that a woman may conceive and give birth to a child of another man rather than her husband. There are also many cases in which one spouse resides for a long period in a remote place or abroad, or both spouses reside in different foreign countries while maintaining married life. Above all, with the development of genetic testing technology, scientific paternity testing is no longer difficult. In today’s circumstances, where absence of blood ties can be directly proven through scientific testing, the need to restrict application of the presumption by indirectly proving absence of blood ties through outward appearance or lack of cohabitation has almost disappeared.
Furthermore, through the 2005 amendment, the person entitled to file an action for disavowal changed from the husband to the spouses, and the filing period changed from within 1 year from the day the child’s birth became known to within 2 years from the day the cause became known. A sufficient period was thereby granted for the spouses to carefully deliberate whether to maintain a parent-child relationship with no blood ties. Nevertheless, if the spouses raise no objection during that period, it may be regarded as an implied intent to accept the already presumed parent-child relationship or not to exercise disavowal. In such a case, there is a need to limit the spouses’ interest in disproving the presumption to align the legal parent-child relationship with the blood relationship; see Constitutional Court en banc decision 2012헌바357. Therefore, it should be understood that a parent-child relationship cannot be denied by an action for confirmation simply because the spouses and child lack a blood relationship, and moreover by proving outward appearance or lack of cohabitation, which is only an indirect means of proof.
(3) On the other hand, as already noted, under Articles 10, 17, and 36(1) of the Constitution, all citizens have the right to pursue happiness and the autonomous decision-making right concerning family relations, and these rights should be respected to the fullest extent unless they infringe on another person’s fundamental rights or public interest. Further, although legal parent-child relationships or family relationships in our society are generally based on blood ties, they are not composed solely of blood ties or necessarily coincide with them. Under our Civil Act, the adoption system, though distinguished from the natural child system, was transformed into an adoption system for the child, and an adopted child without blood ties to the adoptive parents has the same status as their natural child from the time of adoption (Article 882-2(1)). A special adopted child under the special adoption system introduced by the 2005 amendment is regarded as born during the married life of the spouses (Article 908-3(1)), is indicated in the family relation register as the adoptive parents’ natural child, and takes the surname and origin of the adoptive parents. Since a parent-child relationship subject to the presumption can be dissolved only by disavowal, this necessarily presupposes formation and maintenance of a legal parent-child relationship without blood ties. As seen above, even in cases where a child is born after receiving sperm from a third party through assisted reproduction, a social parent-child relationship different from biological blood ties is formed. Thus, while legal parent-child relationships or family relationships may still be said to start from biological blood ties, social parent-child relationships or family relationships unrelated to biological blood ties already exist in our society’s traditions and are accepted and recognized in more diverse ways within today’s social system.
Furthermore, in light of today’s heightened rights consciousness, equality of the sexes, and the highly diversified forms of family in social reality, status-law regulation of children should above all aim at child welfare, and the constitutional demand that the autonomous decisions of the parties to a parent-child relationship should be respected as much as possible must also be heeded; see Supreme Court Order 2018스566 and Constitutional Court en banc decisions 2001헌가9 etc. In light of the ideals of family law and the purpose of the presumption and disavowal provisions, namely prompt determination of status and legal stability, the need to recognize exceptions should be examined from the standpoint of child welfare. As discussed, since parent-child relationship has important value not only in blood ties themselves but also in the substance of social life as parents and children, if a social parent-child relationship has been formed and matured between legally recognized parent and child, there is a need to limit trust in that relationship so it cannot be arbitrarily destroyed by one party or a third party. On the other hand, there are also cases where, beyond scientific proof that there is no blood relationship between the husband and child, no social parent-child relationship has been formed or it has broken down irretrievably so that no interest exists to be protected by the presumption system. Moreover, the Civil Act does not provide a right of disavowal for the child or biological father, who are the direct interested parties. Although the mother’s disavowal right is recognized, it cannot be said to necessarily coincide with the child’s interests. Where the mother and legal father do not raise the child and, due to indifference, do not file disavowal or let the filing period lapse, while the biological father has in fact formed a parent-child relationship by raising the child or there is a high probability that such relationship could be formed, it is difficult to find a justifiable reason to restrict the personality rights and right to pursue happiness of the interested party seeking the truth of the blood relationship, absent special circumstances. In such cases, limiting the application of the presumption may better accord with child welfare.
Accordingly, the traditional limitation theory that recognized exceptions only on the criterion of outwardly apparent circumstances making it impossible for the wife to conceive the husband’s child can no longer be maintained as is. Considering the aforementioned constitutional demands, where scientific proof establishes that there is no blood relationship between the husband and child and no social parent-child relationship has been formed or it has broken down, it should be understood that the parent-child relationship may be denied without an action for disavowal as an exception to the presumption; however, even if absence of blood relationship is scientifically proven, it is reasonable to understand that the parent-child relationship may not be casually denied where a social parent-child relationship exists. Here, social parent-child relationship means a state in which an emotional bond as father and child has formed and the actual circumstances of life are established, such as the father’s intent to play the role of father and to protect and educate the child. In determining this, various circumstances surrounding the family relationship should be comprehensively considered, such as whether the spouses’ marriage continues, whether and for how long there has been a living arrangement that may be regarded as a former family community, whether an emotional bond has formed between father and child, the cause of the breakdown of the parent-child relationship and the parties’ responsibility, the child’s age, the possibility of restoring the social parent-child relationship, and the effect that recognizing the breakdown has on the child’s personality formation and emotions.
(4) Examining the facts discernible from the lower court judgment and the record in light of the above legal principles, as the majority opinion states, in this case the Plaintiff has maintained the parent-child relationship for a long period after Defendant 2’s birth while knowing that he had no biological blood relationship with Defendant 2. Defendant 2, knowing that there was no blood relationship with the Plaintiff, has the intent to maintain a parent-child relationship with the Plaintiff and does not yet know who his biological father is. Although Defendant 2 learned of this when, while the Plaintiff and the non-party were divorcing, he heard the Plaintiff say that Defendant 2 was not his biological child, having lived without knowing that there was no blood relationship with the Plaintiff, he still regards the Plaintiff as his father and is litigating the present claim while hoping that the Plaintiff will remain his father.
If such are the circumstances, it cannot be said that the social parent-child relationship between the Plaintiff and Defendant 2 has been extinguished, nor can it be said that there is no interest to be protected through the presumption provision. Therefore Defendant 2 is still presumed to be the Plaintiff’s natural child under Article 844(1), and it is not permissible for the Plaintiff to seek confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship against Defendant 2, who is subject to the presumption.
Although there are inappropriate aspects in the lower court’s determination, its conclusion dismissing the Plaintiff’s appeal and upholding the first-instance judgment dismissing this part of the action is proper. The lower court made no error affecting the judgment, such as misunderstanding the relevant legal principles or exceeding the limits of free evaluation of evidence.
C. Conclusion
As stated above, although we agree with the majority opinion as to the conclusion of the case, we differ as to the reasons, and therefore state this in our separate opinion.
5. Separate opinion of Justice Min Yoo-sook as to Defendant 1 and dissenting opinion as to Defendant 2
A. Premise for discussion
The parts concerning Defendant 1 and Defendant 2 share many issues. Both Defendants were born while the lawful marriage relationship between the Plaintiff and the non-party remained in force and while they were cohabiting as spouses, but genetic testing revealed no blood relationship with the Plaintiff. However, Defendant 1 was born through artificial insemination using sperm from a third party with the Plaintiff’s consent, while Defendant 2 was born from the non-party’s extramarital relationship. The Plaintiff filed this action seeking confirmation of nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship as to the Defendants, and argued that the presumption under the Civil Act did not apply because there was no blood relationship and because the Plaintiff had azoospermia.
The lower court, as to Defendant 2, held that the effect of the presumption does not apply where the genotype is incompatible, but as to Defendant 1, it took a somewhat inconsistent stance by holding that even though genotype incompatibility was apparent in the third-party-sperm artificial insemination, the child is presumed to be the husband’s natural child if the husband consented.
Accordingly, the Supreme Court is now in a situation where it must make a clear determination as to the scope of the effect of the presumption and the permissibility and scope of any exception.
The majority opinion, in its determination as to Defendant 2, says that even if it is revealed that there is no blood relationship between the child and the father, the child is still presumed to be a natural child, and it devotes the entire majority opinion to explaining the basis therefor, pointing out, inter alia, that because the presumption provision is strictly framed, the father-child relationship is uniformly determined according to Civil Act provisions and cannot be determined through individual and concrete examination. The majority then concludes that since Defendant 2 was born during the marriage of the Plaintiff and the non-party, the effect of the presumption applies even though genotype incompatibility was revealed, and therefore the lower court’s contrary determination is improper.
In other words, the majority takes the position that even where there is no blood relationship, no exception to the presumption is allowed, and then immediately concludes that the presumption applies without further examining whether there are any other exceptions.
However, Supreme Court precedents have adopted the so-called outward appearance theory and have allowed exceptions in certain cases. Because the lower court held, as to Defendant 2, that the effect of the presumption does not apply, if the majority had held that absence of blood relationship does not fall under an exception, it then would have had to determine whether there are cases in which an exception is recognized by precedent or interpretation, and whether this case falls within that scope, before reaching the conclusion as to whether the presumption applies to Defendant 2.
Considering the logical stages of such determination, the majority appears to mean not only that the absence of blood relationship does not fall under an exception, but also that no exception grounds are allowed at all as a matter of interpretation. This is contrary to prior precedents, and this opinion rather takes the position that precedents should be expansively interpreted; therefore, we dissent.
Meanwhile, the concurring opinion says that the majority did not address whether exceptions may be recognized as a matter of interpretation because it did not mention prior precedents. Although we find this difficult to accept, if the majority’s intention is indeed not to express a view on interpretation and application of the precedents concerning exceptions, we state our opinion in the sense that future cases should be interpreted as set out below.
For convenience, we first address Defendant 2, where the general legal doctrine of presumption applies, and then Defendant 1, where the unique doctrine of artificial insemination is at issue.
B. Dissenting opinion as to Defendant 2
(1) Summary of dissent
The lower court held that the presumption under Article 844(1) does not apply to Defendant 2, but that all substantive requisites for adoption were satisfied between the Plaintiff and Defendant 2, and therefore a valid adoptive parent-child relationship was established. The majority opinion and Separate Opinion 1 both conclude that the presumption applies to Defendant 2 without even proceeding to a determination on the effect of adoption.
However, Defendant 2 should be regarded as not subject to the presumption, and the lower court’s determination on adoption is erroneous in that it misunderstood the legal principles concerning adoption effect and implied ratification and failed to conduct the necessary examination.
First, the majority opinion, on the premise that the presumption is strictly applied and that no exception is allowed except by the disavowal action, denies even the area where precedents had allowed exceptions in certain cases.
Although the majority may present a legally superior interpretation, it cannot derive a reasonable conclusion in many cases where there is no parent-child relationship but the family relation register has erroneously registered such relationship and the parties seek to correct it. It is for this reason that, together with two successive improvement legislations easing disavowal requirements, precedents recognized exceptions under the so-called outward appearance theory.
We agree with Separate Opinion 1 to the extent that it pointed out the problems in the majority opinion regarding the permissibility of exceptions and concluded that exceptions should be allowed within a certain scope as a matter of interpretation. However, we differ as to Separate Opinion 1’s presentation of the so-called social parent-child relationship theory, which the Supreme Court had not previously adopted, and as to its view that the presumption applies to Defendant 2.
(2) Whether the presumption applies
(가) The majority says the presumption still applies even though absence of blood relationship has been revealed. But absence of blood relationship is a basic element in allowing exceptions. Rather, the issue here concerns whether the existing exception where the presumption does not apply, formed over time in precedents, should be maintained and, if so, to what extent; in other words, whether the doctrine recognizing cases in which the presumption does not apply under certain requirements should be maintained and what its scope should be.
(나) Supreme Court precedents and their application
The established precedents held that where there are outwardly apparent circumstances making it impossible for the wife to conceive a child of the husband due to lack of cohabitation, such as where one spouse has been abroad for a long period or the spouses are separated due to de facto divorce, the presumption does not apply; see 82므59, 2000므292.
According to those precedents, even where the child is born during marriage and the presumption should apply, if absence of blood relationship is proven by outwardly apparent circumstances making it impossible for the wife to conceive the husband’s child during the conception period, one may exceptionally escape the presumption and correct the status relationship in the family relation register to conform to the truth through an action for confirmation of nonexistence. The reason the precedents allowed exceptions is that in our social reality there are diverse circumstances by which persons lacking true blood ties are registered as parent and child, and there is a need to correct the registration afterward to conform to facts, while the interests surrounding this are diverse and complex, and the rigidity of the presumption provision and the strict filing requirements for disavowal cannot resolve this.
The presumption provision, combined with the disavowal provision, bars a person subject to the presumption from disputing the child’s status relationship if the person with standing does not file suit within the filing period, and thereby produces unreasonable results by requiring that even where the substance of marital and family cohabitation has already disappeared and the parties also seek to escape legal regulation of the parent-child relationship, and there is little legal interest that the presumption was intended to protect, the matter can be rebutted only by the strict disavowal action.
The prior decisions held that it is not in all cases where it is outwardly apparent that the wife cannot conceive the husband’s child, but rather where there are outwardly apparent circumstances due to lack of cohabitation, that the exception is recognized.
Accordingly, through interpretation and application of the outward appearance theory, the legislative purpose of protecting privacy and domestic peace and ensuring the child’s stable status was harmonized with the fundamental rights of the parties seeking to align legal parent-child relationship with truth.
However, because using only lack of cohabitation as the criterion poses problems, it is necessary to expansively interpret the meaning of outwardly apparent circumstances in line with current circumstances.
(3) Exception to the presumption
(가) Reflection of social change
Limiting outwardly apparent reasons solely to lack of cohabitation would make it impossible to reflect changes in the surrounding conditions of adjudication in concrete cases.
The presumption and disavowal provisions have existed since the enacted Civil Act, and the first precedent recognizing an exception was rendered in 1983. At that time, it was normal for spouses to cohabit in one place after marriage, so lack of cohabitation became an outwardly apparent circumstance showing the wife could not conceive the husband’s child, as a means of clearly proving absence of blood relationship without infringing privacy.
However, now divorce rates have increased, social perceptions have changed, and laws and institutions have changed, including stricter divorce regulation. The period from marital breakdown to divorce has become longer. Women increasingly work while living in different regions or countries from their spouses. With genetic testing, scientific paternity testing is possible at low cost and with remarkable accuracy without infringing privacy. In such circumstances, using only lack of cohabitation as an indicator of normal married life or conception possibility does not fit current life patterns or disputes. Thus lack of cohabitation has become a difficult criterion for recognizing exceptions.
The courts, while recognizing the presumption principle, must determine through legal interpretation who may, until when, and on what grounds assert an exception and by what standards it will be accepted, so that parties may escape the presumption situation. This does not negate the presumption’s significance; it is to define, through interpretation, the permissible scope of escape from unjust results contemplated when the presumption was created.
(나) Amendment to the Civil Act and its limits
Amendments have proceeded in the direction of easing disavowal requirements.
The enacted Civil Act set the filing period as 1 year and limited standing to the husband, but this was found unconstitutional. As improvement, the 2005 amendment set the filing period as 2 years from knowledge of the cause and added the wife as standing holder. Notably, it did not limit the filing period to a period after birth.
Later, the Constitutional Court held unconstitutional the provision presuming a child born within 300 days after termination of marriage to be the former husband’s natural child. In response, the 2017 amendment retained the presumption principle but introduced permission requests for disavowal and acknowledgment, allowing exclusion of the presumption by a simpler method for a child born within 300 days after marriage ended.
In particular, Articles 854-2 and 855-2 provide that for such child the presumption applies in principle, but if the family court grants permission requests for disavowal or acknowledgment after considering scientific tests or other circumstances such as long-term separation, the presumption shall not apply. Although limited to a specific period, this reflects a legal doctrine that the scope of non-application can be reasonably set through judicial determination.
The two rounds of improvement legislation show that the need to allow exceptions has become increasingly high. In areas not resolved by the legislation, the need to expand existing precedents arises.
Although the relief scope has broadened, the 2-year filing period may still be insufficient in some cases. In actual family relations, a party seeking disavowal must inevitably prepare for termination of marriage. An action for disavowal is filed on the premise of divorce litigation or agreement divorce. Where a husband learns that the child has no blood relationship and then chooses between agreement divorce and judicial divorce, 2 years may be insufficient before filing disavowal. Family court’s protective role in divorce has been strengthened.
In agreement divorce, the cooling-off period system introduced in 2007 added 3 months if there is a child to be raised. Whether by agreement or judicial divorce, matters concerning custody and child support for minor children must be determined.
Moreover, even after divorce procedures commence, spouses may seek to maintain the family again. If the 2-year period is uniformly applied, the person entitled to file is forced into a dilemma of either filing disavowal within a short period and extinguishing not only the parent-child relationship but also the family relationship, or forever losing the opportunity to disavow by renouncing the right. Such result runs counter to the purpose for which the Civil Act established the marriage and family system through the presumption and disavowal provisions.
The more efforts are made to improve divorce procedures and prevent indiscriminate divorce and family dissolution, the greater the need becomes to allow exceptions proportionately.
The child and biological father, who are direct interested parties, are still denied standing. In many lower-court cases, judgments granting claims for confirmation of nonexistence filed by a child or biological father have become final. The Korea Legal Aid Center for Family Relations submitted an opinion in this case stating that the presumption provision is excessively strict in light of social changes, that it sees many people suffering because they cannot register births, and that the scope of exceptions should be expanded so that parent-child relationships based on true blood ties may be formed while prioritizing child welfare. This shows that, depending on the concrete case, applying the presumption may instead produce results contrary to the original legislative purpose.
(다) Intermediate conclusion
The existing precedents recognizing exceptions under certain requirements should be maintained and expanded. The outwardly apparent circumstances making it impossible for the wife to conceive the husband’s child should be interpreted as including not only lack of cohabitation but also other outwardly apparent circumstances in light of the changes and the amended Civil Act purpose. Which cases fall under this cannot be stated uniformly. The family court should reasonably determine the matter by considering scientific test results, separation and its duration, separate residences or frequent travel, and other circumstances. It may also consider whether the marriage has ended or broken down so that former cohabitation cannot be maintained, the circumstances and process, the attitudes and intent of the persons concerned, whether the claimant is a direct interested party, whether the biological father intends to acknowledge and raise the child, and whether a third party has motives other than establishing true status relations, such as property interests.
(라) Propriety of the lower court’s determination
The part of the lower court’s determination that if a child conceived and born by the wife has a genotype incompatible with that of the husband, the presumption does not apply, is not appropriate. However, the lower court as a whole appears not to have recognized an exception merely on the basis of absence of blood relationship, but rather to have judged that the presumption did not apply by comprehensively considering all the surrounding circumstances revealed in the proceedings, including the substance of the marital relationship, the circumstances by which Defendant 1, who is 4 years older than Defendant 2, was obtained through artificial insemination, the fact that the Plaintiff learned Defendant 2 was not his natural child, and the circumstances leading to the divorce from the non-party, who is the mother of the Defendants. Accordingly, the lower court’s determination denying the presumption as to Defendant 2 is proper.
(4) Effect of adoption by birth registration
(가) The lower court held that all substantive requisites for adoption were satisfied between the Plaintiff and Defendant 2, and that an adoptive parent-child relationship had been established.
(나) Even where a false birth registration of a natural child is filed, the doctrine giving effect to adoption where substantive requisites are satisfied has been maintained since Supreme Court en banc judgment 77다492.
Despite criticism that the precedent lacks a theoretical basis or does not fit the adoption-registration system, it has remained firmly in place. This is because adoption substituted for raising a blood-unrelated child as if a natural child under legal constraints that made it impossible for an adopted child to take the adoptive father’s surname, in a reality negative to adoption. It not only produced results consistent with the welfare of minor children, but also stabilized status relations by preventing third parties from disputing the effect of adoption. The existing precedents sought to ensure the welfare of children, especially minors, by protecting the substance of parent-child relationships such as upbringing and support and by seeking stability in the child’s status relationship, and that value remains today.
(다) However, if the adoption system and legal regulations have changed, one must follow accordingly. The 2005 amendment introduced the special adoption system, reflecting the adoptive parents’ intent to raise the adopted child as their own natural child while requiring strict requisites and procedures. Further, the 2012 amendment provided that permission from the family court must be obtained for adoption of a minor and made adoption without permission a ground of invalidity. The existing precedents also require no ground for invalidity between the parties; therefore, in cases to which the amended Civil Act applies, even if a false birth registration was made with intent to adopt, it would fail to satisfy the requisites absent family court permission and fall within a ground of invalidity. Accordingly, where the amended Civil Act applies, the precedents granting adoption effect to birth registration as to minors will no longer be sustainable. However, since the amended provisions have been in force only from 2013. 7. 1., they do not affect effects arising under prior provisions even after entry into force. Therefore, if all substantive requisites were already satisfied before the amendment took effect, the above doctrine would not apply.
(라) Even where the amended Civil Act does not apply, the change in adoption system and legal regulations is a factor to be considered when applying the precedent’s purpose to a concrete case.
For adoption to be effected, the adoptive father, adoptive mother, and adoptee must each express an intention. Precedents have eased the requirements by recognizing retrospective effect where, even absent statutory agent consent, the adoptee can be regarded as having implicitly ratified the adoption after acquiring capacity.
Even in property law, implied ratification requires circumstances showing that the person fully understood the legal status arising from the act and, based on true intent, acknowledged that the consequences would be attributable to him or her. Merely leaving matters unobjected for a long period while knowing of the defect is insufficient. Even without relying on those doctrines, caution is needed in recognizing implied ratification solely because the person knew of invalid adoption and did not object.
(마) Propriety of the lower court’s determination
The lower court held that the Plaintiff appears to have already known through a hospital examination by no later than around 2008 that Defendant 2 was not his natural child, and that for a considerably long period until around the time of filing this action, the Plaintiff lived together with Defendant 2 without issue while protecting and educating Defendant 2 as a father and continuously maintaining an adoptive parent-child relationship, and on that basis determined that at least until before the application for confirmation of intent to divorce by agreement, all requisites for adoption were satisfied and a valid adoptive parent-child relationship had been established.
According to the lower court’s findings and determination, the application for confirmation of intent to divorce by agreement was made before the amended Civil Act took effect, so the amended Civil Act does not appear to apply.
However, the lower court’s determination is difficult to accept.
According to the facts found, the Plaintiff clearly learned in 2008 that Defendant 2 was not his natural child, so it is hard to see that he had an intent to adopt from the time of birth registration until then. The lower court only found that the Plaintiff did not object until around 2013 or lived with Defendant 2, and it cannot readily be concluded that he thereby implicitly ratified an invalid adoption.
Furthermore, according to the record, during that period the Plaintiff repeatedly pressed his wife as to who Defendant 2’s biological father was, and conflict continued until this action was filed. The Plaintiff applied for confirmation of intent to divorce by agreement on 2013. 6. 28., then after withdrawal filed an application for mediation seeking divorce on 2013. 10. 8., and mediation was established on 2015. 10. 30., resulting in divorce. In the process, he alleges that the fact that Defendant 2 was a child born of an extramarital relationship became known to others, including the wife’s family, and to the Defendants, and that conflict intensified so normal family life could not be maintained.
If so, the Plaintiff’s argument is that, at the time of Defendant 2’s birth registration, he was not certain that Defendant 2 was not his own natural child, and thus registered him as a natural child because he thought so, but by 2008 he clearly knew he was not, and yet spent about 5 years in a situation where he had to choose between ending the marital relationship, which would also affect his relationship with Defendant 2, his spouse, and the other children, or maintaining the marital relationship as is. The lower court should have carefully examined the circumstances and the Plaintiff’s attitude, in addition to the fact that he did not object, and then determined the existence of an intent to adopt and whether there was ratification. The ground of appeal alleging that the lower court misunderstood the legal principles concerning the effect of adoption and implied ratification and failed to conduct the necessary examination is well-founded.
C. Separate opinion as to Defendant 1
(1) Summary
Although we agree with the majority opinion and Separate Opinion 1 as to the conclusion that the Plaintiff cannot deny the parent-child relationship with Defendant 1, we differ as to the reasons. First, we agree with the majority opinion that, in the absence of legislation concerning parent-child relationship of children born through artificial insemination, the presumption under the Civil Act applies. However, we differ from the majority on the scope, whether disavowal is permitted, and its requirements. Next, Separate Opinion 1 is an entirely different view in that it does not find the basis for recognizing the relationship in the Civil Act.
(2) Application of the presumption provision
(가) In Korea, there is no legislation governing artificial insemination and parent-child relationship. In countries that have such legislation, they generally recognize establishment of parent-child relationship between the husband and the child born through artificial insemination on the basis that the mother’s husband consented. However, because there are differences regarding whether disavowal is allowed, and regarding the requirements and manner of consent, it is difficult to find a uniform standard.
(나) In the absence of legislation, there is an aspect in which it is difficult to apply as is the presumption established on the premise of a child conceived through sexual intercourse.
However, the legislative purpose of eliminating the legal protection gap at birth is also valid in the case of artificial insemination, and taking into account that the presumption system for determining father-child relationship has a structure similar to this case where the husband and sperm donor are separate, and further that if the sperm donor is anonymous it is difficult to identify him and impossible to expect acknowledgment, it is appropriate, in third-party sperm donation type artificial insemination, to apply Article 844 between the husband and the born child.
Meanwhile, third-party sperm donation type artificial insemination presupposes from the outset that the child born to the spouses will have no biological blood relationship with the husband. In artificial insemination conducted with the husband’s consent, this is a circumstance already known to and accepted by the spouses, and the auxiliary acts of husband’s consent and artificial insemination or embryo transfer substitute for sexual intercourse. Therefore, in such cases, it is difficult to find the necessity or justification for applying the outward appearance theory as an exception.
(다) However, this legal doctrine applies only where the wife, during marriage, gives birth to a child through artificial insemination using third-party donated sperm with the husband’s consent. In this point, we differ from the majority opinion.
Although the majority expressly said at the outset that it was dealing only with third-party sperm donation type artificial insemination, in the actual reasoning it concludes otherwise that the presumption applies to a child born through artificial insemination during marriage, thus applying the presumption uniformly to all artificial inseminations.
The majority says that legal status does not differ depending on the specific circumstances by which conception occurred, and that there is no reasonable basis to exclude the presumption merely because the child was not born through sexual intercourse. Whether conception occurred through sexual intercourse or artificial insemination is a factor entirely unrelated to recognition of a natural parent-child relationship. There is no doubt that the presumption applies where the wife receives the husband’s sperm during marriage and gives birth through artificial insemination; such case is entirely different from third-party sperm donation type artificial insemination. The reason the presumption issue arises here is not that Defendant 1 was not born through sexual intercourse, but that Defendant 1 has no blood relationship with the Plaintiff.
The majority says that taking biological blood relationship alone as the basis of parent-child relationship is unjust. But whether the core of parent-child relationship can be divorced from biological blood relationship is questionable. Cases where blood relationship exists clearly and cases where it does not exist clearly cannot be regulated in the same way.
Next, this discussion does not apply even to cases in which assisted reproductive methods are used on the wife’s side. Generally, the mother-child relationship is interpreted as a natural parent-child relationship established by childbirth, but with medical advances, if the woman who provided the egg, the woman who actually gave birth by implanting the in vitro fertilized embryo into her uterus, and the woman who requested childbirth through surrogacy are not the same, then the scope of “wife” in Article 844(1) and the scope of “husband” in “presumed to be the husband’s child” must be interpreted and determined under separate legal principles.
(3) Whether disavowal should be permitted as to an artificial insemination child
(가) Since application of the presumption is affirmed as to the establishment of parent-child relationship of an artificial insemination child, the action for disavowal provision must also apply, and accordingly disavowal may be filed.
However, where the husband has consented to artificial insemination, it is interpreted that the natural parent-child relationship cannot be denied by analogical application of Article 852. The husband’s consent is given to the medical act of artificial insemination, but because artificial insemination is inevitably connected to conceiving, giving birth to, and raising the child, the consent should, absent special circumstances, be regarded as intended to recognize the future child’s parent-child relationship.
(나) However, the majority goes further and says that in the absence of other proof, consent should be deemed to have existed, and we differ from the majority on the requirements for recognizing consent.
Since consent has important legal significance, whether consent was given must be recognized by evidence, and neither where consent is not recognized nor where the existence of consent is unclear can consent be presumed or deemed. Also, unless the husband knew of the artificial insemination birth, even if he registered the child’s birth and raised the child believing him or her to be his own child, this cannot be taken as consent. As long as there remains the probability that artificial insemination was carried out on the basis of a consent form prepared without consent or against the spouse’s will, the requirements for recognizing consent must be strengthened, not relaxed.
(4) Separate Opinion 1 says that if a husband and wife had a concurrence of intent regarding the birth of an artificial insemination child and, on that basis, consented to artificial insemination using a third party’s sperm, the child should be regarded as the spouses’ natural child. It also excludes disavowal in such case by saying the spouses’ concurrence and consent cannot be reversed after the fact. The legal doctrine proposed by Separate Opinion 1 creates, by interpretation, a parent-child relationship so firm that it cannot be reversed after the fact where there is concurrence of intent between spouses and birth pursuant to artificial insemination procedures.
The Civil Act does not provide that the effect of establishing a natural parent-child relationship arises solely on the basis of the intent to become a parent. Parent-child relationships form the basis of family relationships and have important status-law effects that serve as the basis for various related legal effects. It is difficult to agree with Separate Opinion 1, which excludes related Civil Act provisions that can be applied in the absence of legislation and seeks, through interpretation, to achieve greater legal effects than the Civil Act anticipates.
D. For the above reasons, although we agree with the majority opinion and Separate Opinion 1 as to the conclusion concerning Defendant 1, we differ as to the reasons. As to Defendant 2, we cannot agree with the majority opinion or Separate Opinion 1.
6. Concurring Opinion of Justice Kim Jae-hyeong to the Majority Opinion
I present an opinion supplementing the majority opinion concerning several questions.
A. Can the presumption provision be applied to an artificial insemination child?
(1) When new circumstances not anticipated by the legislature arise due to changes in society, how the law should be interpreted or applied often raises difficult problems.
Due to the limits of human cognitive and predictive ability, the legislature cannot enact laws while anticipating all concrete cases. Nor can it preliminarily determine the contents of laws to fit a wide variety of cases in response to changing social reality and various problems. Therefore, the law must continue to maintain vitality as a norm regulating real life not only for cases specifically contemplated at the time of enactment, but also for cases not so contemplated. If the law were applied only to the specific cases anticipated by the legislature, then as society changes and science and technology develop, the law would easily lose vitality and require constant new legislation.
Even where a case arises that the legislature had not anticipated, the courts cannot refuse to adjudicate. Where neither written law nor custom exists as the standard in a civil case, the judge must adjudicate according to reason and logic (Civil Act Article 1). The courts, in order to determine whether existing laws can be applied to new cases not anticipated by the legislature, must utilize various methods of legal interpretation to ascertain the meaning of the law and carefully examine whether it can be applied to the new case.
Generally, unless contrary to the ordinary meaning of the text, the courts must respond to changes and developments in the times by interpreting the law through systematic and logical methods considering legislative purpose, enactment and amendment history, harmony with the legal order, and relations with other laws. It is not desirable to simply conclude that a case requires judge-made law and solve it by new doctrine merely because the legislature had not anticipated it, without carefully examining whether existing law can be applied or applied by analogy.
(2) As the majority notes, at the time the Civil Act was enacted it was not conceivable that a child could be born through artificial insemination, and therefore no express provision could be established concerning attribution of parent-child relationship. Even after children began to be born through artificial insemination, no legislation was enacted to determine attribution. Thus, there may be a legal vacuum.
However, to resolve this issue, one must begin from the Civil Act’s provisions determining parent-child relationships. The Civil Act does not have an express provision excluding the application of the presumption to an artificial insemination child. The presumption provision is framed very broadly, saying that a child conceived by the wife during marriage is presumed to be the husband’s child. Therefore interpreting it as generally applying to the father-child relationship of a child conceived by the wife during marriage accords with textual interpretation.
The Civil Act legislator anticipated that such child might not have blood ties with the husband, and contemplated application of the presumption even in such a case. Even if a child born through artificial insemination using a third party’s sperm has no blood relationship with the husband, applying the presumption to such child cannot be regarded as contrary to the statutory text, legislative intent, or purpose. Thus the fact that the legislator did not anticipate artificial insemination birth when establishing the presumption cannot, by itself, exclude its application.
The meaning of statutory text is not fixed. It may change according to socioeconomic changes and scientific and technological development. Objects not previously expected to fall within the text may, with time and social change, be included. Even where the wife conceives through a new method such as artificial insemination by receiving third party sperm, it is reasonable today to regard this as included in the concept of conception, a requirement for the presumption. Because the provision does not specify a narrow subject such as natural conception but instead states the rule broadly, it can be seen as flexibly responding to artificial insemination.
If the presumption does not apply to artificial insemination, at minimum analogical application should be affirmed. There are similarities between the case contemplated by the legislature and the case of an artificial insemination child, and in light of the system and legislative purpose, applying the presumption by analogy can be justified. However, the legal effect does not differ depending on whether the presumption is applied directly or by analogy. It is not the case that analogical application must always be considered merely because a case was not anticipated; as above, in light of the textual form of the provision, applying the presumption to an artificial insemination child is a reasonable method of interpretation and application.
B. Can parent-child relationships be determined according to social parent-child relationship?
(1) Separate Opinion 1 states that where no social parent-child relationship has been formed between legally recognized parent and child, or where such relationship has broken down and there is no interest to be protected by the presumption system, and where scientific proof establishes that there is no blood relationship between the mother’s husband and the child due to genotype incompatibility, an exception should be recognized. Through this, it takes the existence or nonexistence of social parent-child relationship as the standard for determining parent-child relationship. However, this standard lacks legal basis and cannot serve as a standard.
(2) Legal interpretation should, as a principle, faithfully follow the ordinary meaning of the text, and further should aim to produce the most reasonable interpretation for the concrete case by additionally using systematic and logical methods considering legislative purpose, enactment and amendment history, harmony with the legal order, and relations with other laws. However, if the statutory text itself is composed of relatively clear concepts, other methods are in principle unnecessary or may be used only limitedly; see Supreme Court Decision 2006다81035.
As the majority opinion notes, the presumption provision determines whether the presumption applies solely by reference to conception during marriage, and does not distinguish application on other grounds. The factors are marriage, conception, and birth. Since these are all determined at birth, it cannot be said that whether the presumption applies changes according to circumstances arising after birth. Treating the existence or nonexistence of a social parent-child relationship, which is a circumstance after birth, as a ground for exception is not consistent with the Civil Act’s approach of determining application based on the time of birth.
(3) Circumstances that a social parent-child relationship was not formed or has broken down after birth are not only difficult to function as a consistent standard, but interpreting them as grounds on which the presumption does not apply also runs counter to the purpose of the provision.
The social parent-child relationship proposed by Separate Opinion 1 contains many evaluative elements and is difficult to operate as a consistent standard. Also, breakdown of such relationship may be intentionally created by the parties and is mutable. Even if it appears broken down at the time of trial, it may be restored. Separate Opinion 1 says that where a child has formed a social parent-child relationship with the biological father, an exception should be recognized so that legal parent-child relationship with the biological father can be secured; however, the social parent-child relationship between child and biological father may also be mutable.
Furthermore, it is not reasonable to treat such criteria as grounds for exception to deny the legally presumed parent-child relationship. The presumption provision has the legislative purpose of maintaining family peace and promptly stabilizing the child’s legal status. Moreover, the Civil Act limits standing and filing period in the disavowal provision, giving the presumption stronger force than other legal presumptions, and this was also intended to protect the legal interests of persons concerned through stability of status relations. Since there is no express exception and interpretation contrary to the text in a direction opposed to legislative purpose should be restrained.
Germany’s recognition of the biological father’s right to disavow even as to a presumed child, and its limitation of that right where there exists a social family relationship between legally formed father and child, can also be understood from this perspective. The German Civil Code prescribes disavowal by statute and limits eligible applicants and filing period for stability of the child’s legal status (Sections 1600 and 1600b). It allows not only the father, mother, and child, but also the biological father to exercise disavowal, but unlike the others, the biological father may exercise it only on the premise that no social family relationship exists between the legally formed father and child. It permits the biological father’s disavowal only where no social family relationship exists. Thus in Germany the concept of social family relationship is introduced to protect the social family relationship formed pursuant to the presumption and to maintain legal stability of status relations. This places social family relationships above blood relationships by protecting the legal relationship under the presumption. Conversely, allowing denial of the legally presumed parent-child relationship on the basis of breakdown of social parent-child relationship, regardless of who seeks denial, may instead emphasize clearly established biological parent-child relationships or blood relationships, and therefore cannot be accepted as interpretation of our Civil Act.
C. Why the majority opinion did not change the existing precedent
The Civil Act presumes that a child conceived during marriage is the husband’s natural child, and recognizes an action for disavowal as a means to rebut this presumption while strictly limiting standing and filing period.
The enacted Civil Act allowed only the husband to file disavowal within 1 year from the day the child’s birth became known. Since the husband often cannot know within that period whether the child is his natural child, it was necessary to ease the requirements.
The Supreme Court, under the enacted Civil Act, held that where there are outwardly apparent circumstances making it impossible for the wife to conceive the husband’s child due to lack of cohabitation, such as where one spouse has been abroad for a long period or the spouses are separated due to de facto divorce, the presumption does not apply; see 82므59 and 2000므292. The reason was that the presumption was established for family peace on the premise that the spouses are carrying on normal married life, and that applying it even where that premise is not satisfied and allowing denial only by the strict disavowal action would run counter to the purpose of the system and could produce unjust results. The precedents can be understood as recognizing the above problems and developing a theory that preserves the purpose of the presumption while preventing unjust results.
There are arguments both for and against these precedents. Some argue that not only in lack of cohabitation but also where genotype incompatibility is present, the presumption should not apply, while others argue that the precedents should be changed so the presumption applies without limitation to children born during marriage. The majority opinion does not mention these precedents and does not address this issue.
The issues in this case are ① whether the presumption can be applied to an artificial insemination child and ② whether an exception can be recognized on grounds other than those recognized by existing precedents.
As stated above, the presumption still applies even in the case of genotype incompatibility. Whether existing exceptions recognized by precedents under the outward appearance theory should be maintained, or whether the precedent should be changed so the presumption applies without limitation, are matters not directly related to the concrete resolution of this case, and such arguments are not included in the Plaintiff’s grounds for appeal. The majority opinion, without addressing whether to change the precedents, limited its determination to whether the presumption applies to the Defendants under the issues discussed above.
D. How should the problems arising from limiting standing in the action for disavowal be resolved?
The Civil Act has eased the strictness of the action for disavowal through amendment. Article 847(1), amended by Act No. 7427 on 2005. 3. 31., set the filing period as 2 years from the day the husband or wife became aware of the cause, so the period does not run until they know the truth of the blood relationship, and grants a practical opportunity to deny the presumption by providing time for careful deliberation. Articles 854-2 and 855-2, newly established by the 2017 amendment, while allowing the presumption to apply in principle to a child born within 300 days from the date the marital relationship ended, allow the mother and her former husband to file permission requests for disavowal and the biological father to file a permission request for acknowledgment, thereby allowing the presumption to be excluded by a simpler method than an action for disavowal.
Nevertheless, arguments continue that the scope within which the presumption does not apply should still be expanded. The most important reason is that the disavowal provision does not allow the child or biological father, who are direct interested parties, to exercise the right. If disavowal is not allowed for the child without exception, the child’s personality rights may be seriously infringed, or there may be a marked discrepancy between the legally presumed father-child relationship and the socially recognized father-child relationship, and yet the opportunity to correct this may be blocked from the outset.
As a matter of legislative policy, it is desirable to amend the Civil Act and grant disavowal rights to interested parties including the child, subject to certain requirements. Before such legislation, it is necessary to seek a solution at the interpretive level. One opinion suggests further expanding exceptions where the presumption does not apply, but this risks damaging the form of parent-child relationship the Civil Act sought to create through the presumption and disavowal provisions, and is difficult to accept as legal doctrine. Here, we propose that for husbands or wives recognized as having standing under the disavowal provision, the parent-child relationship be determined according to that provision, and for children and others not recognized as having standing, parent-child relationship be determined by an action for confirmation of existence or nonexistence of natural parent-child relationship through systematic and rational interpretation of the current Civil Act.
Interpretation and application of statutes in concrete cases is an inherent authority and mission entrusted to the courts, and if a reasonable method of interpretation that considers both connotation and extension of the statutory text can be achieved, the courts should adopt such a constitutionally conforming interpretation.
Under the current Civil Act, which recognizes standing to file an action for disavowal in the husband or wife, they may, upon learning that the child is not a natural child, file an action within 2 years and remove the legal parent-child relationship. However, unless paternity is disavowed, the child cannot escape the legal parent-child relationship under the presumption provision by means of an action for disavowal even if he or she learns that he or she is not a natural child. Meanwhile, the Civil Act provides, in addition to the disavowal action, an action for confirmation of existence or nonexistence of natural parent-child relationship (Article 865) as a means to correct discrepancies when the substantive legal parent-child relationship and the legal parent-child relationship in the family relation register do not match. Under Article 865, a person having an interest in the natural parent-child relationship may file an action for confirmation of nonexistence on the ground of other reasons.
Since the husband or wife may file disavowal under the disavowal provision where there are grounds, seeking confirmation of nonexistence on such grounds is not permitted because it violates Article 865. However, although the child is the direct party in interest subject to the effect of the presumption provision, standing is not recognized for the disavowal action. Yet if the Civil Act is interpreted in a direction that completely excludes the opportunity for the child, the direct party in interest, to align the legally presumed relationship with biological truth merely on this ground, it would seriously restrict the child’s personality rights, self-determination, right to pursue happiness, and fundamental rights concerning marriage and family relations based on dignity and sex equality. This is not the proper method the Supreme Court should adopt. Accordingly, it is necessary to examine whether the unreasonable result may be removed through the action for confirmation recognized by the Civil Act. If, even according to ordinary meaning, it is possible to interpret that the child subject to the presumption may file an action for confirmation of nonexistence of natural parent-child relationship, and such result does not run counter to the legislative purpose of the presumption and disavowal provisions, then through such interpretation it may be a reasonable method to realize the child’s constitutional rights by allowing an opportunity to escape the consequences of the presumption.
First, in the child’s case, although grounds for disavowal exist, the child cannot file an action for disavowal, so seeking confirmation on such grounds is not, in light of Article 865’s text, naturally prohibited. That said, it should not be understood that anyone with an interest in the child’s parent-child relationship presumed as natural child may seek confirmation of nonexistence under Article 865. The legislative purpose of restricting disavowal can be found in early stabilization of status relations, child welfare, and prevention of third-party interference in the marital family, thereby protecting the privacy of the child and spouses and the peace of the marital family. Considering the legislative purpose of the presumption and the purpose of strictly prescribing procedure and period in the disavowal action, interested parties who may dispute the status of a child born during marriage and subject to the presumption should be recognized only within the extent that does not undermine that purpose. Therefore, the child subject to the presumption should be understood as able to file an action for confirmation because the child has a direct interest, but a person with a status-related or property-related interest should not, absent special circumstances, be understood as being able to seek confirmation of nonexistence.
Even if the child may file an action for confirmation, it cannot be said to be allowed without limitation. The disavowal provision sets a filing period requiring the husband or wife to file within 2 years from the day the cause became known. Even where a child subject to the presumption files an action for confirmation, absent special circumstances, the filing period should be limited by analogically applying the disavowal provision, and the starting point should be when the child became aware of the cause, or when the child became of age if the cause was learned during minority.
In this way, if a child subject to the presumption receives a final judgment declaring nonexistence of natural parent-child relationship, the res judicata effect of that judgment extends to third parties as well pursuant to Article 21 of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Registration, etc. of Family Relationships, so that no one may assert, in or out of litigation, a claim contrary to the effect of disavowal and the presumption effect disappears. However, even a child who can file an action for confirmation with disavowal effect cannot immediately assert an exception to the presumption or deny its effect in the absence of such a judgment. In other words, unless there is a final judgment granting such confirmation, a child subject to the presumption cannot file an acknowledgment action against the biological father, nor can the biological father acknowledge such child.
It is desirable to resolve the problems arising from the strict limitation of standing in the disavowal action by allowing the effect of the presumption to be rebutted within the extent that the purpose of the presumption or the disavowal action is not nullified.
I present the above supplemental opinion to the majority opinion."}
