(2) However, since Non-Party 2’s parents and others strongly opposed the marriage on the ground that Non-Party 1’s conduct was not upright, Non-Party 2 had been delaying the marriage registration, but in around 1963 he suffered a large loss from securities investment and left home around 1963. 4.경, concealing his whereabouts for several months; during that time, on 1963. 9. 3., Non-Party 1, using Non-Party 2’s seal without authorization, filed a marriage registration with Non-Party 2, and also filed birth registrations for the Plaintiffs as their natural children between them, so that Non-Party 1 and the Plaintiffs were each entered in Non-Party 2’s 호적 as his wife and children.
(3) Accordingly, Non-Party 3, the mother of Non-Party 2, filed a petition with the Seoul Family Court against Non-Party 1 and Non-Party 2 seeking a ruling confirming that their marriage was void; meanwhile, Non-Party 1 filed, with the Seoul Family Court Case No. 65NEO911, an application for mediation against Non-Party 2 and Non-Party 3 seeking an order designating Non-Party 1 as the custodian of the Plaintiffs and requiring them to jointly and severally pay 2,500,000 won as consolation money because they had made it impossible for her to live together with Non-Party 2.
Thereafter, when a judgment confirming the invalidity of the marriage between Non-Party 2 and Non-Party 1 was rendered, Non-Party 1 appealed, then received a judgment dismissing the appeal, and again filed an appeal, but while the case concerning the claim for confirmation of invalidity of marriage was pending before the Supreme Court, on January 17, 1966, in the above mediation case, a settlement was reached to the effect that "the relationship between Non-Party 1 and Non-Party 2 as a man and a woman shall be dissolved; it shall be confirmed that no natural parent-child relationship exists between the Plaintiffs and Non-Party 2; Non-Party 1 shall bear all responsibility for the care and other matters concerning the Plaintiffs; Non-Party 1 shall hereafter be barred from making any and all judicial claims relating to the Plaintiffs; Non-Party 2 and Non-Party 3 shall transfer to Non-Party 1 the land and building located in Jangchung-dong, Jung-gu, Seoul; and Non-Party 1 shall withdraw the appeal in the case concerning the claim for confirmation of invalidity of marriage." Pursuant thereto, Non-Party 1 withdrew the appeal in the case concerning the claim for confirmation of invalidity of marriage, the judgment of invalidity of marriage became final and conclusive, and the Plaintiffs became children born out of wedlock.
(4) On June 1, 1967, after the judgment of invalidity of marriage had become final and conclusive, Non-Party 2 married Defendant Intervenor 1, and between them, gave birth to Defendant Intervenor 2 on March 18, 1968 and Defendant Intervenor 3 on June 26, 1970, while, against the Plaintiffs, he filed a claim for confirmation of invalidity of acknowledgment with the Seoul Family Court Case No. 67DEU877; in response, Non-Party 1, in the capacity of the Plaintiffs’ special representative, filed with the Seoul Family Court Case No. 68DEU236 a petition against Non-Party 2 seeking an order designating Non-Party 4, the Plaintiffs’ maternal grandmother, as the custodian of the Plaintiffs and requiring payment of the costs of their care.
Accordingly, on September 6, 1968, a ruling was rendered confirming that "the acknowledgment (birth registration) made by Non-Party 2 to the Head of Jongno-gu Office, Seoul Special Metropolitan City, as of September 3, 1963, identifying the Plaintiffs as his children is invalid." In the case concerning the petition for designation of custodian, etc. filed by Non-Party 1 on behalf of the Plaintiffs, on September 19 of the same year, a judicial settlement was reached to the effect that "it is confirmed that the Plaintiffs are not the natural children of Non-Party 2, Non-Party 2 shall pay 3,500,000 won to the Plaintiffs, and the Plaintiffs shall make no further monetary claim." And as the ruling confirming invalidity of acknowledgment became final and conclusive, the Plaintiffs were removed from Non-Party 2’s family register, and by the establishment of separate family registers, each was entered as the head of a family, with the father column left blank and the mother designated as Non-Party 1.
(5) After the above judicial settlement had been reached, Non-Party 1 married another man and cut off relations with the Plaintiffs; meanwhile, Non-Party 2, while substantially performing the role of the Plaintiffs’ father by, inter alia, giving them school expenses so that they could study abroad and attending their weddings, died on November 30, 1994, and the Plaintiffs filed the instant action for acknowledgment on January 4, 1995.
2. Regarding the grounds of appeal on the preliminary defense portion
The court below, in response to the intervenors’ assertion that the instant claim for acknowledgment conflicts with the res judicata effect of the final and conclusive ruling confirming invalidity of acknowledgment and of the mediation and judicial settlement that included confirmation that no natural parent-child relationship exists between the Plaintiffs and Non-Party 2, and that it also violates the principle of estoppel in light of the contents of that mediation and judicial settlement, and further constitutes an abuse of the right of action as the exercise of a right of action that had already ceased after de facto waiver or extinction of the right to claim acknowledgment, held that the final and conclusive ruling confirming invalidity of acknowledgment clearly had as its subject matter a confirmation that the voluntary acknowledgment by birth registration was invalid because, despite the fact that Non-Party 2 himself had never acknowledged the Plaintiffs as his natural children or filed their birth registrations, the family register was entered as if such act had been done by Non-Party 1; accordingly, its res judicata effect arises only to the extent that the voluntary acknowledgment by birth registration of Non-Party 2 is invalid, and its effect does not extend even to whether a natural parent-child relationship exists between Non-Party 2 and the Plaintiffs; therefore, the effect of that final and conclusive ruling does not extend to the instant claim seeking judicial acknowledgment on the premise that a natural parent-child relationship exists between the Plaintiffs and Non-Party 2, and that a claim concerning confirmation of the existence or non-existence of a natural parent-child relationship, which corresponds to a Category A domestic relations litigation case under the current Family Litigation Act, by its nature concerns matters over which the parties cannot freely dispose, and thus even if mediation or judicial settlement is reached thereon, it cannot have legal effect (see Supreme Court Decision 65DA139, 140 rendered on April 6, 1968); therefore, the above mediation or judicial settlement has no effect with respect to confirming that no natural parent-child relationship exists between the Plaintiffs and Non-Party 2, and there is no room for res judicata to arise, and moreover, the right to claim acknowledgment cannot be waived, and even if waived, no effect can arise (see Supreme Court Decision 85MEU70 rendered on January 20, 1987), so it cannot be said that the Plaintiffs waived their right to claim acknowledgment or forfeited it due to the mediation or judicial settlement, and thus the instant claim cannot be said to violate the principle of estoppel or to constitute an abuse of rights, and accordingly rejected all of the intervenors’ arguments.
Examining the record, the above determination by the court below is correct, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality such as misapprehension of the law concerning res judicata, issue preclusion, loss of rights through lapse, waiver of rights, or the principle of estoppel. The grounds of appeal on this point cannot be accepted.
3. Regarding the grounds of appeal on the merits
According to the reasons of the judgment below, the court below, on the basis of the commissioned genetic testing results and factual inquiry results among the evidence it adopted, found that the possibility that the deceased Non-Party 2 was the biological father of the Plaintiffs could not be ruled out, and that the probability of paternity was, in the case of Plaintiff 2, as low as 88.029% and as high as 99.9999999998%, and, in the case of Plaintiff 2, as low as 91.891% and as high as 99.99999999995%; then, comprehensively considering the factual circumstances noted above, it recognized that the Plaintiffs were the natural children of the deceased Non-Party 2 born between Non-Party 1 and the deceased Non-Party 2, and granted all of the Plaintiffs’ claims for acknowledgment in this case.
Comparing the relevant evidence with the record, such factual findings by the court below are acceptable, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality such as violation of the rules of evidence, factual error due to insufficient deliberation, omission of judgment, or misapprehension of the law concerning the burden of proof. The grounds of appeal on this point are likewise not accepted.
4. Therefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing parties. The judgment is rendered as per the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

question: Which of the following statements regarding the subjective elements of the offense is correct? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law)
A: With the intent to kill, if the actor assaults the victim (act (a)), and when the victim loses consciousness and goes limp, mistakenly believes the victim to be dead and buries the victim in sand for the purpose of destroying evidence (act (b)), and it is found that the victim died from act (b), since the direct cause of death is act (b), attempted murder is established.
B: In order for an actor’s conduct to qualify as necessity, it is sufficient that the actor has only awareness of the emergency situation of necessity; an intent to avoid the danger is not also required.
C: Where a person, with the purpose of harming another, instigates a person who does not have the purpose of harming another to commit perjury, under the principle of accessory dependence, the offense of instigating perjury, rather than instigating perjury for the purpose of harming another, is established.
D: If a witness, being mistaken, testifies to content contrary to objective facts without awareness that it is contrary to his or her own memory, intent to commit perjury can be recognized.
E: Where an actor who accidentally received a mistaken remittance from a trading company that is in litigation over a claim for payment of the price of goods refuses to return the mistakenly remitted money with the intent to exercise a lawful right of setoff against the price of the goods, the establishment of the intent of unlawful appropriation, which is an element of embezzlement, may be denied.

{"[2021DO2088]": "We examine the 상고이유.

1. Summary of the Facts Charged  
The gist of the facts charged in this case is as follows.  
The Defendant was an inside director of B Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “B”), a 주류 company, and had been engaged in 주류 supply transactions with the Victim. The Defendant, having filed a civil action against the Victim seeking payment of 주류대금, received and held KRW 4,700,000 on September 30, 2019, remitted by the Victim to an account in the name of B managed by the Defendant, during the civil dispute. However, the above amount was money the Victim had intended to remit to Co., Ltd. C, and was remitted to the Defendant by mistake of 계좌번호, and the Defendant was obligated to return the above amount after being notified by the Victim through text message on October 1, 2019 that the above amount had been remitted by mistake. Nevertheless, without any 합의 with the Victim concerning 상계 and 정산, the Defendant unilaterally set off and settled KRW 1,108,310, being the amount of the 주류대금 claim asserted by the Defendant, and then refused to return the money and embezzled it.

2. Judgment of the Court Below  
The court below held that, with respect to the money mistakenly remitted by the Victim to the Defendant, so long as a 보관관계 under the principle of 신의칙 is recognized between the Defendant and the Victim, the Defendant could not unilaterally set off such money as with money entrusted by limiting its purpose or use; accordingly, it judged the facts charged in this case to be guilty on the ground that the Defendant’s act constitutes “반환의 거부,” an element of the crime of 횡령, and that the intent of 불법영득도 also recognized.

3. Judgment of the Supreme Court  
a. Since “반환의 거부” as prescribed in Article 355(1) of the Criminal Act means an act of expressing an intention to exclude the owner’s rights over the thing held in custody, in order for “반환의 거부” to constitute 횡령, it is insufficient that a person who keeps another’s property in custody merely refused to return it; by comprehensively considering the reason for the refusal to return and the subjective intentions, the refusal to return must be such that it may be viewed as equivalent to an act of 횡령. The intent of 불법영득 in the crime of 횡령 refers to the intention of a person who keeps another’s property in custody to dispose of it as if he or she were the owner, without just title, contrary to the purpose thereof; therefore, even if return is refused, if there is a 정당한 reason for the refusal to return, it cannot be said that there was intent of 불법영득 (see Supreme Court Decision 98DO126 dated July 10, 1998, Supreme Court Decision 2000DO637 dated September 4, 2002, Supreme Court Decision 2014DO11552 dated February 26, 2015, etc.).

b. Examining the following circumstances, as discernible from the reasons of the judgment of the court below and the record, in light of such legal principles, the Defendant’s act of refusing to return the portion corresponding to B’s claim against the Victim among the money remitted to the account in B’s name by the Victim’s mistake may be viewed as an exercise of a valid right of 상계; accordingly, it is difficult to accept as is the court below’s determination that the Defendant’s refusal to return constitutes an act of 횡령 and that the intent of 불법영득 is recognized.

(1) Where money has been mistakenly remitted to and deposited in a deposit account by error, a 보관관계 under the principle of 신의칙 is established between the recipient and the remitter (see Supreme Court Decision 2010DO891 dated December 9, 2010, Supreme Court en banc Decision 2017DO17494 dated July 19, 2018, etc.); however, absent special circumstances, this alone does not mean that the money remitted by mistake by the remitter is identical to money expressly entrusted by the entrustor with a specified purpose and use, nor can it be evaluated that the recipient’s exercise of a set-off right against the remitter is contrary to the original intent of the entrustment on the ground that the remitter entrusted the recipient with affairs involving the receipt and payment of money.

(2) In light of the progress of the related civil case, B appears to have held a claim for payment of goods corresponding to the amount of the refusal to return against the Victim as of the time of the refusal to return described in the facts charged in this case. There also appears to be no material or circumstances suggesting that, at that time, the above claim for payment of goods of B and the Victim’s claim for return of unjust enrichment were not in 상계적상, or that B’s exercise of the right of set-off constituted a violation of the principle of 신의칙 or an abuse of rights.

(3) The Defendant returned, on the day after the remittance, the remainder of the KRW 4,700,000 mistakenly remitted, excluding the amount corresponding to B’s above claim for payment of goods in the amount of KRW 1,108,310, and even with respect to the KRW 1,108,310, appears to have sufficiently made clear to the Victim, who requested its return, the intention to exercise the right of set-off using B’s above claim for payment of goods as the automatic claim. In this manner, when examining the reason for and subjective intention behind the Defendant’s refusal to return the money corresponding to the amount of the above claim for payment of goods, it is difficult to conclude that the Defendant refused to return it with intent of 불법영득.

c. Nevertheless, the court below judged the facts charged to be guilty by regarding the Defendant’s refusal to return as equivalent to an act of 횡령 in the crime of 횡령 and recognizing the intent of 불법영득. The judgment of the court below contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the act of 횡령 and the intent of 불법영득 in the crime of 횡령 and by failing to conduct the necessary review.

4. Conclusion  
The judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices, as stated in the disposition."}

{"[80DO306]": "In considering the grounds of appeal submitted by each defense counsel for the Defendants and by Defendant G himself (including supplementary grounds in part), for convenience in this judgment all of the above grounds of appeal shall collectively be referred to as the “Grounds of Appeal,” and they shall be considered item by item, broadly divided in the following order.

5. 대법원판사 Jeong Tae-won의 의견
6. 대법원판사 Seo Yun-hong의 의견

Section 1. 공소기각의 결정을 간과한 위법

Among the Grounds of Appeal, it is argued that even based on the facts stated in the indictment, there is no statement of specific facts concerning the purpose of subverting the Constitution, the riotous acts, and the contents of the conspiracy, which are constituent elements of the crime of insurrection, or concerning the division of execution in the co-principal offense of murder; thus, because the facts charged are not specified, an order dismissing the prosecution should have been entered pursuant to Article 373(1)4 of the Military Court-Martial Act, but the lower court overlooked this and thereby erred in misunderstanding the above legal principles. We shall first consider this point.

Upon review, this point was already lawfully considered by the lower court. In addition, the facts charged against the Defendants, as organized from the indictment in this case and the applications to amend the indictment made on two occasions, are sufficiently specified on their face to be recognized as the relevant offenses, and it is admitted that they are specifically stated. Further, as to the murder of Defendant C, the indictment clearly charges co-principal liability by conspiracy; accordingly, in that case, the omission of facts concerning the division of execution in co-principal liability cannot be deemed a defect. Therefore, this argument is without merit.

Section 2. Procedural illegality

1. 불고불리의 원칙 위반

Among the Grounds of Appeal, it is argued that, according to the indictment and the application to amend the indictment, Defendant G was prosecuted for killing T and U with the purpose of subverting the Constitution, but the lower judgment found Defendant G to have killed six persons, namely B, T, V, W, X, and U; this, it is argued, is a violation of the principle of accusation and adjudication and thus a violation of law. We consider this argument.

Upon review, according to the application to amend the indictment lawfully granted at the first trial date in the lower court, it is clear, as argued, that Defendant G was prosecuted for having killed T and U, among the six deceased persons in this case, for the purpose of subverting the Constitution. However, in the reasoning of the lower judgment, in the conclusion portion concerning the facts of the offense of murder with insurrectionary purpose, the court stated that from around 19:40 to 20:05 on the same day, former President B, the said T, the said V, the said W, the said X, and the said U were each caused to die, thereby the Defendants jointly murdered the above victims for the purpose of subverting the Constitution. This appears, on its face, to have committed the illegality alleged. Nevertheless, the lower court had previously stated that on October 26, 1979, around 19:40, Defendant G, after the other Defendants had fired at the above deceased persons, received at around 20:05 that day an instruction from Defendant E to carry out a confirmation shot on persons not yet fully dead and agreed to participate in that killing. Not only that, but the lower court also stated that, with respect to the shooting pursuant to that instruction, it was done by firing one shot at the said W lying fallen, two shots at the said V, two shots at the said T groaning, and one shot at the said U lying fallen and groaning. In view of this point, although the expression in the conclusion portion of the lower judgment is somewhat inaccurate, it is still recognized that the lower court judged within the scope of the prosecution. The argument is without merit.

2. “공개재판” 위반

Among the Grounds of Appeal, it is argued that the court-martial of first instance, at the second trial date on December 8, 1979, conducted the defense counsel’s statements and questioning of Defendant A in closed session without satisfying the prescribed requirements, and also, at the ninth trial date on December 18, 1979, effectively prohibited public access and proceeded with Defendant A’s final statement without even entering a decision of closure; thus, it is argued that the closed proceedings were plainly illegal in their grounds and procedure. We consider this argument.

Upon review, according to the record, at the second trial date on December 8, 1979, during the defense counsel’s cross-examination of Defendant A, the court ordered a closed proceeding on the ground that Defendant A, as former Director of the Central Intelligence Agency, had performed important duties concerning foreign intelligence and domestic security intelligence, security affairs pertaining to state secrets, insurrection, foreign relations, the investigation of crimes prescribed in the National Security Act, the Anti-Communist Act, and similar laws, and the coordination and supervision of intelligence and security affairs, and the content of the defendant’s statements in this court pursuant to the defense counsel’s cross-examination substantially includes matters that may interfere with the security or public order of the State. It then proceeded in camera thereafter. This was based on Article 67 of the Military Court-Martial Act, which provides that the oral proceedings and judgment in trial shall be public, provided however, that where public order may be disturbed, morals harmed, or where necessary for military secrecy, the military court may decide not to hold them publicly. Even in light of the record, the reason is fully understandable. Therefore, the first-instance court’s measure was proper and cannot be said to have been mistaken. Accordingly, this portion of the argument is without merit.

Further, whether any stage of the trial proceedings was public is to be recorded in the trial transcript pursuant to Article 85(2)5 of the Military Court-Martial Act. Article 89 of the same Act provides that matters recorded in the trial transcript as procedural acts on a trial date are proved by that transcript alone. Thus, the public or private nature of the proceedings on December 18, 1979, the ninth trial date in the first instance, can be established only by the trial transcript in this case. The first-instance ninth trial transcript states in the column for public or private that the trial was public in court. Therefore, it can be recognized that the proceedings on that date were conducted in a public courtroom. Accordingly, this argument also lacks merit.

3. 신문제한의 위법

Among the Grounds of Appeal, it is argued that the first instance and the lower court, though under Article 344 of the Military Court-Martial Act they could limit examination only to the extent that the essential rights of parties to the litigation were not harmed, nevertheless restricted examination and statements whenever specific references were to be made in the course of examining Defendant A concerning the motive and purpose of this act, the domestic political situation immediately before the act, and the inevitability of the act, and also frequently imposed limitations during the examination of Defendants E and F; this, it is argued, constituted a grave infringement of the Defendants’ and counsel’s right of defense beyond the permissible bounds of examination restriction. We consider this argument.

Upon review of the first-instance and appellate trial transcripts, it can be recognized that the first instance and the lower court afforded the above Defendants necessary and sufficient opportunities to make statements, and that each defense counsel was granted the necessary right to examine the Defendants and other parties to the litigation; further, it is sufficiently recognized that each defense counsel had necessary and sufficient opportunities to defend the Defendants, which were realized, and that each Defendant had a full opportunity to make final statements. In particular, in the case of Defendant A, from the content of the Defendant’s statements in response to examinations by the prosecutor, defense counsel, and legal officer in the first-instance and appellate courts, as well as the supplemental statement of reasons for appeal submitted by Defendant A himself, and the statements of reasons for appeal and grounds of appeal submitted by his counsel, it can be recognized that the defense content alleged by the appellant is sufficiently reflected. Therefore, the contrary argument lacks merit.

4. 퇴정명령의 위법

Among the Grounds of Appeal, when questioning Defendant C and others at the third trial date on December 10, 1979, the first-instance court, invoking Article 343(2) of the Military Court-Martial Act, ordered Defendant A to withdraw from the courtroom on the ground that he could not make sufficient statements in Defendant A’s presence; this, it is argued, was done without just cause solely upon the application of the prosecutor, and furthermore, when Defendant C’s statement ended in that case, Defendant A, who had been withdrawn, should have been brought back into the courtroom and informed of the substance, and Defendant A should have been allowed to question Defendant C directly, but instead the proceedings were simply closed without Defendant A being brought back into the courtroom that day; this is said to be illegal. We consider this argument.

Upon review, according to the first-instance third trial transcript, before the examination of Defendant C at the said third trial date, the first-instance court, ex officio, ordered the remaining Defendants including Defendant A to withdraw from the courtroom on the ground that they were deemed unable to make sufficient statements in the presence of co-defendants. This measure was based on Article 343(2) of the Military Court-Martial Act. In light of the record, this was reasonable. It is true, as argued, that after Defendant C’s statement ended at that date, the proceedings were closed without Defendant A being brought back into the courtroom. However, according to the first-instance fourth trial transcript, when the first-instance court resumed and, at the fourth trial date, the legal officer informed the parties in the courtroom, which included all defendants in this case including Defendant A and all their counsel, of the substance of the previous court hearing on Defendant C, and asked the parties for their views, the parties stated that they had no particular opinion; this is clearly shown in the record. Further, according to the first-instance sixth trial transcript, it is clearly shown in the record that Defendant A’s assigned counsel O and Y cross-examined Defendant C on behalf of Defendant A. Therefore, this argument lacks merit.

5. 증인신문절차의 위법

Among the Grounds of Appeal, first, according to the witness examination record of Z adopted by the lower court, it is clear that Defendant A was not allowed to participate in the examination of that witness. This, it is argued, violated the law guaranteeing a defendant’s right to participate in witness examination and, through that, the right of cross-examination. Second, it is argued that, in examining witnesses, there was no service of summons by the prescribed procedure under Articles 106 through 108 of the Military Court-Martial Act; moreover, in some cases, witnesses were made to wait in advance before the prosecutor had even applied for evidence, and then were taken up and examined immediately upon application; this, it is argued, was not only a procedural violation but a grave illegality depriving the Defendants and their counsel of the opportunity to prepare for cross-examination. We consider this argument.

Upon review, first, according to the first-instance trial record, at the eighth trial date at which all the Defendants in this case and their counsel were present, regarding witness Z who failed to appear, the first-instance court instructed the legal officer that he would conduct the examination outside the courtroom and ordered the attendance of the relevant persons. Thereafter, on December 17, 1979, legal officer AA examined the witness at the Army Headquarters Judge Advocate General’s Office, where Defendant C and his counsel and the counsel for Defendants A and D were present. In the manner of that witness examination, it cannot be said that Defendant A was not notified and thus was denied an opportunity to participate. Moreover, the witness’s testimony primarily concerned the criminal facts of Defendant C, so it cannot be said that there was any illegality in the procedure. In addition, according to the same trial record, at the ninth trial date resumed on December 18, 1979, the first-instance court, after the legal officer informed the courtroom that witness Z had been examined, presented the substance and asked the parties for their opinions; the parties stated that they had no particular opinion, as clearly shown in the record. Therefore, even if there were a mistake as alleged, the Defendants and their counsel stated at the evidence examination that they had no particular opinion, so the mistake would be cured by waiver of the right to object. Accordingly, this part of the argument is without merit.

Second, according to the first-instance trial record, after the first-instance court selected eight witnesses at the sixth trial date, it examined the two selected witnesses who appeared at the seventh trial date, and at the eighth trial date it newly selected nine witnesses present at the court and examined those witnesses and the five witnesses selected earlier who appeared. Also, one witness examination was conducted outside the courtroom by legal officer AA on December 17, 1979, all of which is clear from the relevant trial transcripts and witness examination records. Under the proviso of Article 192 of the Military Court-Martial Act, witnesses present in court may be examined without summons, so it cannot be illegal that the nine present witnesses were not summoned. Nor can it necessarily be faulted that those witnesses were examined immediately upon application. As to the remaining witnesses, although summons procedures should have been taken, no trace of the issuance of summons can be found in the record. However, after examining those witnesses and the witness outside the courtroom, the first-instance court afforded the Defendants and their counsel the opportunity to state their opinions in court or at the next trial date, and they stated that they had no particular opinion. Moreover, it is clearly shown in the record that the Defendants and their counsel conducted sufficient and necessary cross-examination of those witnesses. Therefore, the defect of non-issuance of summons cannot be said to be a case affecting the outcome of the judgment, and this portion of the argument also cannot be accepted.

6. 변호인 없이 개정한 위법

Among the Grounds of Appeal, in military court cases, counsel is mandatory under Articles 62 and 315 of the Military Court-Martial Act, and therefore proceedings cannot be opened without counsel’s appearance. Nevertheless, on January 22, 1980, at the first trial date, as a measure under Article 416 of the Military Court-Martial Act rather than severance of trial, the lower court opened proceedings with only Defendants C and G present and without the appearance of Defendants A, E, and F and their counsel, and is alleged to have illegally examined matters concerning the motives and circumstances of the co-defendants’ offenses. We consider this argument.

Upon review of the appellate trial record, after notifying Defendants A, E, and F and their counsel that the first trial date was set for January 22, 1980, the court later re-designated and notified the trial date as January 23, 1980. Then, at the first trial date on January 22, 1980, the court, pursuant to Article 416 of the Military Court-Martial Act, deemed that some of the Defendants including Defendants A, E, and F need not appear at trial and did not order their appearance, but proceeded with the hearing with only Defendants C and G present. Article 416 of the Military Court-Martial Act is only the provision that in appellate proceedings under the Military Court-Martial Act, the appeal instance is not a de novo trial of the first instance, but rather a post hoc review of specific factual and legal issues in the first-instance judgment, and thus as a rule the defendant need not appear at appellate trial dates. It is not a provision allowing only some co-defendants to appear selectively, as in this case, and excusing the appearance of the others. Therefore, the above measure of the appellate court was mistaken. However, at the continued second trial date on January 23, 1980, the legal officer informed the substance of the important matters of the previous trial hearing, and thereafter sufficient opportunity for cross-examination was afforded. Moreover, the record shows that the first instance had already conducted sufficient hearings on the matters alleged in the appeal grounds, and at the first appellate trial date there is no indication that new matters were examined on that point. Accordingly, the error was not such as to affect the outcome of the judgment. The Supreme Court decisions cited by the appellant are not apt to this case. Thus, this argument also cannot be accepted.

7. 변호권의 박탈

Among the Grounds of Appeal, the Defendants’ lineal family members and spouse have, under Article 59 of the Military Court-Martial Act, an independent right to appoint counsel. Thus, even if the defendant himself refuses to argue, the right of counsel appointed by the lineal family members and spouse does not extinguish. Nevertheless, counsel AB and others appointed by Defendant A’s lineal family members and spouse were denied entry into the courtroom by military police serving as courtroom order personnel pursuant to the judge’s order at the first-instance fifth trial date on December 12, 1979, and it is argued that thereby their right to counsel was deprived, and that the court committed illegality in failing to decide on the objection to this point. We consider this argument.

Upon review, even if, pursuant to Article 59(2) of the Military Court-Martial Act, the defendant’s lineal family members and spouse may independently appoint counsel, the appointing party is one who independently exercises the appointing right of the principal, so the effect of the appointment extends to the principal, and the principal must be understood as being able to revoke the appointment. In this case, according to the first-instance fourth trial transcript, while the hearing at the fourth trial date proceeded under the participation of privately retained counsel including attorneys AB and others appointed by Defendant A’s mother and spouse, Defendant A stated that from now on he refused the defense by the private defense team for this defendant. At that time the legal officer informed him that the military court requires counsel and, if the privately retained counsel must be dismissed, the military court must decide to appoint assigned counsel. Defendant A then stated that he would revoke all privately retained counsel for himself, and that he wanted assigned counsel. This is clearly shown in the record. Therefore, the above private counsel were lawfully revoked, and the fact that they were later denied entry to the courtroom as counsel at the first-instance fifth trial date on December 12, 1979, cannot be regarded as deprivation of the right to counsel. Nor can it be said that any illegality occurred merely because the objection thereto was not decided. The argument is without merit.

8. 공판조서의 미비와 열람등 사권의 박탈

Among the Grounds of Appeal, even if the Military Court-Martial Act does not have a provision like Article 54 of the Criminal Procedure Act that trial transcripts must be promptly prepared within five days after each trial date, considering Articles 89, 86, and 64 of the Military Court-Martial Act, etc., the trial transcript in military court proceedings should also be prepared before the next trial date or, at the latest, before the factual hearing ends. Nevertheless, it is argued that the first instance and the appellate court did not promptly prepare the trial transcripts, thereby effectively depriving counsel of the right under Article 64 of the Military Court-Martial Act to inspect and copy the transcripts, etc. We consider this argument.

Upon review, the Military Court-Martial Act does not contain a provision like Article 54 of the Criminal Procedure Act, which sets a statutory period for preparing trial transcripts. Of course, military court trial transcripts must also be prepared promptly, but one cannot definitively say by when they must be completed. In particular, even the statutory period set by the Criminal Procedure Act is only a directive provision, and merely failing to complete the transcript within that period cannot by itself be regarded as rendering the trial transcript void. Therefore, no fault can be found with respect to the timing of preparation of the first-instance and appellate trial transcripts; nor can it be said that there was illegality in depriving the right of inspection and copying of transcripts. The gist of the argument is that it concerns the defendants’ right of defense. Upon review of the first-instance and appellate trial records in this case, it is recognized that the defendants’ right of defense was fully protected; accordingly, this argument cannot be accepted.

9. 재판의 독립성 침해

Among the Grounds of Appeal, it is argued that the first instance and appellate court pressed ahead with the hearing as though there were a fixed, predetermined schedule under the aforementioned unlawful procedures infringing the defendants’ right of defense and right to counsel, and that even during the hearing, there were cases in which notes of contact from outside were publicly and repeatedly handed to the judges through the back door behind the judges’ bench; this, it is argued, violated Article 102 of the Constitution and Article 28 of the Military Court-Martial Act, which guarantee judicial independence. We consider this argument.

As to the arguments alleging that the above first-instance and appellate trial procedures were illegal, we have already found them to be without merit. Even in light of the record, it is not recognized that the factual hearings in the first instance and appellate court were pressed ahead under some fixed schedule as alleged. Rather, the record only shows that the first instance conducted sufficient factual hearings eight times across the second through ninth trial dates, and the appellate court did so three times across the first through third trial dates, while ensuring the defendants’ right of defense and right to counsel. No other illegality is found. Furthermore, there is absolutely nothing in the record suggesting that contact notes were delivered to the judges during the hearing, and especially whether their content infringed judicial independence is wholly unknown. This point is too abstract and fabricated to require further discussion. Therefore, the argument lacks merit.

Section 3. Prosecutor-prepared suspect-interrogation record의 “임의성” 문제

Among the Grounds of Appeal, it is argued that the suspect-interrogation records concerning the Defendants prepared by the prosecutor were merely an extension of the records prepared by the military police investigators because, at the time of the prosecutor’s interrogation, the Defendants were physically and mentally exhausted by numerous acts of torture at the joint investigation headquarters under martial law, and in particular Defendant A made statements involuntarily, under the prosecutor’s earnest persuasion, while his consciousness was dim due to aggravation of his chronic liver disease; or because the prosecutor conducted the interrogation at the place where the military judicial police had investigated after receiving the case, under a state in which access and communication with counsel and family were completely prohibited, and the record content was the same as the military judicial police records except for legal refinement, so that it lacked “voluntariness.” It is argued that the lower court nevertheless used this as evidence of guilt, thereby committing an error of law concerning evidentiary capacity or a defect for failure to provide reasons, and also erred by omitting consideration of the grounds of appeal. We consider this argument. This point is related to the argument below that the fact-finding violated the rules of evidence, and for convenience it is considered separately.

Upon review, in general, the absence of voluntariness in a statement means that the person being interrogated by an investigative authority did not make the statement under free conditions because of threats, torture, or other means. The determination of voluntariness is made within a reasonable scope by the free conviction of the judge without violating the rules of experience. It suffices that the adjudicating panel makes a reasonable judgment in all respects of the litigation process—namely, the preparation and content of the document, the defendant’s explanation and demeanor, the prosecutor’s elucidations, and the testimony of witnesses involved in the preparation of the document. On that basis, the record shows the following, and the lower court’s use of the prosecutor-prepared records as evidence was proper, since voluntariness is admitted in light of the totality of the circumstances. Therefore, this part of the argument lacks merit.

Section 4. 범죄구성요건에 관한 위법

1. “국헌문란”의 목적

Among the Grounds of Appeal, the “국헌문란” prescribed in Article 91 of the Criminal Act, as the purpose element of the offense of murder with insurrectionary purpose and attempted insurrection, ultimately means everything that unlawfully destroys the State’s political basic order itself. The political basic order of our country is, needless to say, a liberal democratic political system; therefore, only acts that substantially or formally destroy the principle of popular sovereignty and the people’s fundamental freedoms and equality would constitute subversion of the Constitution. Accordingly, the overthrow of a specific government or cabinet, or an act of shouting slogans of overthrow, or whether the means of overthrowing is violence, or the killing of a specific constitutional organ as a natural person and the planning of succession or improvement thereof, would not fall under this.

First, in the case of Defendant A, the Yushin system, by its establishment and continuance alone, was not only an illegal criminal state in which sovereignty was usurped, but its content and operation produced a continuing condition that destroyed the political basic order of a democratic state. Therefore, for Defendant A, the killing of the President, a natural person, was unavoidably done according to a plan long prepared for the restoration of democracy. Even if not so, since after this offense he intended to enact a democratic constitution and organize the National Assembly and Government by democratic methods, there was no purpose to subvert the Constitution.

Second, in the case of Defendant C, it is difficult to conclude, merely because he killed T, the head of the Presidential Security Service, who was not even a state organ established by the Constitution, that he had a purpose of “subverting the Constitution” like the co-defendants; and as to Defendant C, neither his own statement nor his external behavior can be said to show such purpose.

Third, in the case of Defendant D, he merely thought that only a few persons would be killed and the President abducted in this offense, and the killing of security officer V and the like, which he admits was done pursuant to the order of his superior, would not amount to subversion of the Constitution. Moreover, Defendant A’s explanation also states that he reached this offense in order to restore liberal democracy, so it cannot be said that there was a purpose to subvert the Constitution.

Fourth, in the case of Defendants E, F, and G, the Defendants were merely security guards or drivers of the Central Intelligence Agency restaurant and, having no choice, blindly and mechanically carried out the orders of Defendant D, the chief responsible person there. They could not even imagine the specific harm and consequences. In particular, Defendant G did not know of the murder of the President or even of its plan. Nevertheless, the lower court found, contrary to Defendant C’s explanation, that the facts it held satisfied the purpose of subverting the Constitution, and as to the other Defendants, it found that they had carried out riots or killings with the purpose of subverting the Constitution, on the ground that they knew a state of national upheaval had occurred. It is argued that this was a fact-finding without evidence, a violation of the rules of evidence contrary to logic and experience, a failure of hearing, and a defect for lack of reasons; or that the legal principles concerning the purpose of subversion of the Constitution in the offense of murder with insurrectionary purpose and attempted insurrection were misunderstood. We consider this argument.

(1) First, we examine the legal principles concerning the purpose of “국헌문란.”

Article 91 of the Criminal Act provides that in this Chapter, “purpose of subverting the Constitution” means, among other things, abolishing the functions of the Constitution or laws without following the procedures prescribed by the Constitution or laws, or overthrowing by force a state organ established by the Constitution or making the exercise of its functions impossible. This ultimately means unlawfully destroying the political basic order prescribed by the present Constitution or laws. As argued, it does not necessarily have an extra-legal meaning, and certainly does not mean changing to a communist, monarchical, or dictatorial system. Of course, killing only a natural person who is a specific state organ, or planning his succession, does not fall under it. Further, since the crime of insurrection is a crime with a specific purpose, the general principles concerning crimes with specific purpose apply. The purpose belongs to matters requiring strict proof and must be direct, but it cannot be said that it requires a desire or will for the result to occur, nor does it require definite knowledge; a conditional awareness is sufficient, see Supreme Court decision dated April 2, 1968, 68DO61.

(2) Next, we examine the lower court’s factual findings on this point regarding the Defendants.

(a) Part concerning Defendant A

The lower judgment stated the following as the facts of Defendant A’s “purpose of subverting the Constitution”: while performing his duties as Director of the Central Intelligence Agency, Defendant A’s plans for stabilizing the political situation repeatedly failed, exposing his incompetence in carrying out his duties, and after being reprimanded by former President B, rumors of a dismissal for taking responsibility circulated, causing him to feel insecure in his position. Meanwhile, although he resented the President’s greater trust in T, then head of the Presidential Security Service, who was junior to him and younger, despite T’s arrogant attitude and interference in matters beyond his authority, he planned to seize power after killing the President, and, for secrecy, independently devised the concrete plan for the act. After assassinating the President, he planned to declare martial law on the ground of national security and public disorder, to use the authority and organizational power of the Central Intelligence Agency to take control of the martial law forces and suppress the situation by force, to constitute a revolutionary committee that would oversee legislative, judicial, and executive powers, to assume the chairmanship himself and secure a basis of power, and then to run for President. Examining the important basis of this conclusion from the evidence lawfully admitted and cited by the lower court, the court could properly find the intent element from the Defendant’s own statements and surrounding circumstances.

Here, Defendant A’s statements, Defendant C’s statements, and the other lawfully admitted evidence are enough to support the finding that the Defendants had the purpose of unlawfully destroying the political basic order prescribed by the present Constitution or laws. Therefore, as no illegality alleged in the appeal is found in the lower judgment, all arguments are without merit. However, with respect to this point, the opinions of Justices Min Mun-gi, Yang Byeong-ho, Im Hang-jun, Kim Yun-haeng, and Seo Yun-hong are set forth in Section 11 below.

2. “폭동”

Among the Grounds of Appeal, the insurrectionary act under Article 87 of the Criminal Act is punished according to the degree of participation in the riot when the act was committed for the prescribed purpose. In such case, “riot” means a combination of a number of persons with some organization that uses violence or intimidation to the extent of disturbing the peace of a locality, and such riot must bear a means-end relationship to the purpose of insurrection. However, first, the Defendants in this case cannot be said to constitute a combination of a number of persons with any organization; second, it cannot be found at all that they used the above violence or intimidation, nor did they reach the degree of disturbing the peace of a locality; and third, although the Defendants’ acts as found by the judgment below cannot be said to bear a means-end relationship to the purpose of subverting the Constitution, the lower court recognized the facts as found and punished them for murder with insurrectionary purpose and attempted insurrection. It is argued that this constitutes misinterpretation of law concerning “riot” in the crime of insurrection, violation of the rules of evidence, and failure of hearing. We consider this argument.

Upon review, “riot” as an element of Article 87 of the Criminal Act means a number of persons combining to commit violence or intimidation. In such case, the combination of many persons requires some degree of organization, but the number cannot be specified. Also, the degree of violence or intimidation must be such as to disturb the peace of a locality; when that degree is reached, the offense is consummated, and when it is not reached, it becomes an attempt. Further, as argued, the riot must bear a means-end relationship to the purpose of insurrection. In this case, even when reviewing the evidence lawfully cited by the lower court in light of the record, the lower court’s factual findings on this point are proper. The above Defendants easily combined based on their positions, trust, and personal relationships as recognized from the record, and their division of roles was clearly determined, so it may be recognized as organized. The gunfire, etc. described in the lower judgment constitutes violence or intimidation as a riot. However, it cannot be said that this reached the extent of disturbing the peace of a locality, though the lower court also held it to be an attempt on the same grounds. On the other hand, according to the record, some of the Defendants were preparing for a gun battle with the Blue House security guards after the above gunfire, and further clashes between military units due to cooperation or opposition were anticipated; if it had come to that, it would undoubtedly have been sufficient to disturb the peace of a locality. In light of the purpose to subvert the Constitution as discussed above, it cannot be denied that the riot in this case bore a means-end relationship to the purpose of insurrection. Meanwhile, the lower judgment found and punished Defendant C as an attempted major participant in the insurrection, and Article 87(2) of the Criminal Act defines a “major participant” broadly to include, for example, those responsible for supply, accounting, liaison, communications, sanitation, general affairs, and similar duties. Defendant C’s original mission falls within a major role in this insurrection case, and it is possible for such a major role to involve no violence or intimidation at all.

Therefore, since no illegality alleged in the appeal is found in the lower judgment, all arguments are without merit. However, on this point, separate opinions by Justices Min Mun-gi, Im Hang-jun, and Kim Yun-haeng concerning all six Defendants, and by Justices Yang Byeong-ho and Seo Yun-hong concerning Defendant C, are set forth in Section 11 below.

3. “가담”

Among the Grounds of Appeal, Defendant C was not in a hierarchical status of superior and subordinate with Defendant A as a state official and thus cannot be said to have joined a group for carrying out the insurrectionary acts in this case. Moreover, there was no conspiratorial agreement regarding mutual communication in the group for carrying out insurrection. Nevertheless, the lower court held that Defendant C joined the group when he received instructions from Defendant A, the leader, to keep security, as if he had joined the group. This, it is argued, was a fact-finding without evidence, or there was a failure of hearing and contradiction in reasons, and it violated the Supreme Court precedent on co-principal liability. We consider this argument.

Upon review, as determined in the above items, Defendant C also clearly participated in this insurrection. Reviewing the evidence lawfully cited by the lower court in light of the record, one can recognize Defendant C’s original acts concerning the attempted major participation in insurrection, and these were indispensable for carrying out the insurrectionary acts in this case. As such, they themselves provide important factual material for the alleged participation, and considering the evidence cited by the lower court, the lower court’s factual findings on this point are proper. The fact that Defendant C was not in the hierarchical status alleged vis-à-vis Defendant A, the leader, cannot be said to obstruct the above factual findings. Also, as expressed in Defendant A’s statement to the prosecutor, Defendant C cannot be said not to have had sufficient communication of intent with Defendant A while agreeing to perform the original mission. Therefore, the lower judgment contains no illegality alleged in the appeal, and this argument also lacks merit.

4. “살해”

Among the Grounds of Appeal, in light of the record in this case, the deceased T’s gunshot wound, inflicted by Defendant A’s gunfire progressing from the front of the right shoulder joint toward the lower left, was a fatal wound; and Defendant G fired two shots only after T had already died. Also, the deceased U died from a fatal gunshot wound to the front of the right chest wall and a gunshot wound to the right scapular area, causing cardiac injury and death by cardiac tamponade; afterward, Defendant G fired one shot causing a blind-ended wound to the right buttock, which had no relation to U’s fatal injury. Nevertheless, the lower judgment found Defendant G guilty and punished him for the offense of murder with insurrectionary purpose. It is argued that this violated the rules of evidence by finding facts of killing without evidence or misunderstood the legal principles of murder. We consider this argument.

According to the reasoning of the lower judgment, the lower court recognized as to Defendant G responsibility for the killing of two of the six deceased persons in this case, T and U. The various lawfully admitted pieces of evidence cited by the lower court show that T and U were alive until immediately before the shock caused by Defendant G’s action and were completely killed by that gunfire. In murder, the object is a living person, and whether the victim had the capacity to survive is irrelevant. Where independent acts clearly caused the result of death, there is no inconsistency in punishing each act as a consummated offense. Therefore, no illegality such as alleged can be found in the lower court’s factual findings or reasoning process. Accordingly, this argument lacks merit.

5. 내란의 실행착수 및 기수시기

Among the Grounds of Appeal, the crime of insurrection becomes consummated when a riot is initiated for the purpose of subverting the Constitution and the riot reaches consummation, regardless of whether the purpose of subverting the Constitution has been attained. In this case, if the President, his chief of security, and the escort guards were murdered for the purpose of subverting the Constitution, that would amount to a riot sufficient to disturb the peace of a locality, and the crime of insurrection would have reached consummation regardless of whether the constitutional-subversion purpose was achieved. Therefore, Defendant C’s conduct in this insurrection is a post-offense act not punishable, or otherwise the execution had not yet commenced. Nevertheless, the lower court found Defendant C guilty of attempted major participation in insurrection. It is argued that the lower court misunderstood the legal principles concerning the commencement of execution and consummation of the crime of insurrection, or committed violations of the rules of evidence and contradiction in reasons. We consider this argument.

Upon review, it is true, as argued, that the crime of insurrection may be consummated after the group action as a riot has begun, regardless of whether the purpose of territorial usurpation or subversion of the Constitution has been achieved. However, the riot must have reached the extent of disturbing the peace of a locality before consummation occurs. In this case, the riotous acts described in the lower judgment alone cannot be said to have reached the extent of disturbing the peace of a locality, so it is not proper to say that the crime of insurrection in this case was consummated. Further, as for the concept of violence or intimidation as riot conduct, this is the broadest possible concept, and the conduct of preparing for or assisting such acts is comprehensively understood as riot. In this case, the state of armed guarding by Defendant F pursuant to Defendant C’s instructions, the state of surveillance by Central Intelligence Agency personnel, and the state of waiting of security vehicles at Army Headquarters, together with the facts discernible from the record by other lawfully cited evidence of the lower judgment, collectively show that the riot did not end after the Gungjeong-dong restaurant gunfire but continued. In particular, Defendant G’s confirmation killing took place after Defendant C had participated in the insurrection, so it cannot be said that Defendant C merely participated in an unpunishable post-offense act. Also, the appellate court’s measure of regarding the riot as having commenced execution when the riotous act began is proper. Therefore, the lower judgment has no illegality such as alleged, and this argument lacks merit.

6. “증거은닉”

Among the Grounds of Appeal, it is argued that, as the elements of the offense of concealment of evidence, only where the objective requirement that the evidence concern another person’s criminal or disciplinary case and the subjective requirement of intent to conceal it are satisfied can the act be punished. Yet Defendant H did not know that the items in question were evidence used in the offense of killing the former President and T’s party, and also had no intent whatsoever to conceal those items. Nevertheless, the lower court upheld the first-instance finding of guilt for concealment of evidence against Defendant H. It is argued that this violated the rules of evidence or constituted a failure of hearing or a misunderstanding of the legal principles concerning concealment of evidence. We consider this argument.

Upon review, it is true, as argued, that the offense of concealment of evidence is constituted when a person subjectively recognizes evidence relating to another person’s criminal or disciplinary case and conceals it. Reviewing the various pieces of evidence lawfully admitted by the lower court in light of the record, Defendant H’s statements and Defendant E’s statements, together with the other evidence, are sufficient to support the first-instance court’s factual finding and legal application as upheld by the lower court. Therefore, this argument lacks merit.

Section 5. 살인죄의 공동정범에 관한 위법

Among the Grounds of Appeal, the lower court held that Defendant C conspired with Defendant A to kill T. However, co-principal liability is, in essence, based on two or more persons jointly, in mutual cooperation, executing their common criminal intent, and to commit a crime with the intention of acting jointly requires not only a communication of intent but also a concrete disclosure of the contents, means, and method of that conspiracy. In addition, beyond such communication of intent, there must be a fact of joint execution as an objective constituent element. Further, in its original form co-principal liability is principally a form of execution co-principal liability, while conspiracy co-principal liability is a ceremonial form in which a person participates only in the conspiracy and does not perform the constituent facts at all, yet is held to the same criminal responsibility as the executor. It arose in actual judicial practice as a theory of accomplice liability where the substantive principal plans the crime behind the scenes and causes subordinates or persons under his control to carry out the execution, making it impossible to treat it as mere instigation or aiding and abetting. Therefore, mere awareness of the crime or communication of intent is insufficient; the word “conspiracy” means a fairly high degree of consultation such as discussing the execution of the crime and determining even the role of the executor. As to a conspirator who does not undertake the execution act, there must be a subjective intent to realize his own crime through the executor. In this case, the conversation or behavior between Defendants A and C in the garden at the restaurant cannot by itself be definitively taken as a proposal to commit murder jointly or as assent thereto, and even the lower court’s explanation cannot be taken to imply that there was intent to kill or communication of such intent; nor is there evidence to support it. Moreover, Defendant C, unlike Defendant A, did not share the execution role when Defendant A killed the chief of security; rather, it appears that he attempted to restrain Defendant A from committing murder. Nevertheless, the lower court recognized Defendant C as a co-principal in the offense of murder and punished him accordingly. It is argued that the lower court thus found facts without evidence, violated the rules of evidence, and committed a defect for lack of reasons and failure of hearing; and further, it misunderstood the law concerning co-principal liability and omission crimes. We consider this argument.

Upon review, since the lower court clearly applied conspiracy co-principal liability to Defendant C concerning the murder of the deceased T, there is no need to consider further the arguments premised on execution co-principal liability. It is a precedent of this Court that in co-principal liability, even if one does not directly participate in the execution after conspiring to commit the offense, one cannot avoid co-principal liability for the acts carried out by other co-conspirators, and in conspiracy co-principal liability, conspiracy means communication of intent among two or more persons to cooperate and realize their common criminal intent. As argued, the conspirator who does not undertake the execution act must have a subjective intent to realize his own crime through the executor; of course, but it is not necessarily required that he be the substantive principal behind the scenes who plans the crime and causes a subordinate or controllable person to carry it out.

In this case, reviewing the evidence lawfully admitted by the lower court in light of the record, the lower court’s factual findings and reasoning on this point are proper. However, if one quotes the important evidence recognized from the record, Defendant C’s statements and Defendant A’s statements do show mutual communication and consent to some extent, and the lower court could infer conspiracy from the totality of the circumstances. Therefore, there is no illegality such as alleged. Accordingly, this argument lacks merit.

Section 6. 중지미수에 관한 위법

Among the Grounds of Appeal, the lower court’s holding, in relation to the attempted major participation in insurrection against Defendant C, that the facts of opposition by the Prime Minister and the Ministers of Home Affairs and Justice cannot necessarily be said to constitute the reason for the failure of the insurrection, and that the fact of pressure by Blue House Chief Secretary Z cannot be said to be a decisive obstacle to insurrection, and in addition there is no evidence to support these points; whereas in fact Defendant C, if he had wanted to help Defendant A after 23:00 that day, could have done so, but instead it was clear that he had him arrested of his own accord. Nevertheless, the lower court found him guilty of attempted major participation in insurrection. It is argued that there was a violation of the rules of evidence, failure of hearing, and misunderstanding of the law concerning abandonment of attempt, and also that the lower court failed to determine the defense on the above purport and thus committed a defect for lack of reasons. We consider this argument.

Upon review, if the various pieces of evidence lawfully admitted by the lower court are examined in light of the record, the lower court’s action on this point is proper. Therefore, the above argument is plainly without merit. The lower court’s important basis, including the prosecutor statements of Defendant C, Defendant A, and the testimony of witness Z, shows that the late-stage collapse of the plan was due to the failure of security maintenance and the Cabinet’s resistance, and Defendant C’s change of attitude and eventual arrest of A were inconsistent with a theory of completed withdrawal or voluntary abandonment that would exempt him. Thus the argument also lacks merit.

Section 7. 위법성조각사유

1. 정당행위

(1) “저항권” 이론

Among the Grounds of Appeal, the “right of resistance,” which has been discussed under natural law by many scholars and is now generally recognized by modern constitutional theory as having even an actual positive-law basis, should be recognized as a natural right with or without express constitutional provision. It is the right that ultimately applies, whether passive, active, violent, or nonviolent, when no other means of remedy exists, for the maintenance of the constitutional order of liberal democracy and the protection of fundamental human rights. In this case, the Yushin system, in its establishment and operation, was an anti-democratic legal order and an anti-human-rights system, so in restoring it, no other lawful remedial procedure was possible institutionally or practically. Therefore, Defendant A and D’s offenses in this case fall within the exercise of the above right of resistance. It is argued that the lower court rejected this application, thereby misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the right of resistance and lawful acts prescribed in Article 20 of the Criminal Act, and that Supreme Court decision 74DA3323 dated April 8, 1975, should be changed. We consider this argument.

This Court has previously held, in substance, that the assertion of the so-called right of resistance is a claim to rights within a supra-positive natural-law order that disregards the existing positive legal order, and under that premise it is interpreted as an attempt to justify acts disregarding the existing constitutional order. Within the scope of positive law premised on the existing constitutional order, the exercise of judicial power charged with maintaining the State’s legal order cannot accept an argument that invokes a supra-legal concept of right to justify acts contrary to the current positive law by disregarding the existing constitutional order.

On the other hand, even if one accepts the argument that, in constitutional theory of modern constitutional liberal democratic states, the so-called right of resistance as a natural right arising from natural law should be recognized as an existing right whether or not it is prescribed in the Constitution or other positive law, as long as that right of resistance does not have a basis in positive law and rests only on natural law, a judge cannot invoke it as a judicial norm. Moreover, even among scholars who acknowledge the existence of the right of resistance today, their views differ widely as to the content of its concrete concept or its requirements for establishment, so it cannot be said to be unified; in the end it cannot escape being called a vague and abstract concept. Since in our Constitution and laws there is no provision concerning the right of resistance at all, we cannot but hesitate all the more to adopt and apply this theory as a standard for adjudication at the present stage in our country. Therefore, there is no need to change the above precedent of this Court, and the argument that there is an error of law in the lower court on this point cannot be accepted. However, on this point, Justices Min Mun-gi and Im Hang-jun have separate opinions.

(2) 정당한 직무집행

Among the Grounds of Appeal, the facts found in the lower judgment concerning attempted major participation in insurrection against Defendant C—namely, security maintenance, prohibition of troop deployment, report to the Prime Minister, and recommendation to the Ministers of Home Affairs and Justice to declare martial law and the reasons therefor—were all the best measures to deal with an emergency situation, an unexpected national crisis that fell upon him as Chief Secretary to the President, and therefore constitute legitimate performance of official duty under Article 20 of the Criminal Act. Nevertheless, it is argued that the lower court overlooked this point, committing an error of law concerning lawful acts and a failure of hearing, and also omitting consideration of the grounds of appeal submitted by that Defendant’s counsel. We consider this argument.

Upon review of the record, the above argument is nothing more than a false explanation offered by Defendant C in order to escape responsibility for the attempted major participation in insurrection charge against him. Rather, the above acts by Defendant C are all recognized as actions taken to actively join, respond to, and support the offense of Defendant A, the leader of the insurrection. Therefore, there is no error of law or failure of hearing by the lower court on this point. And since there is no error of law or failure of hearing on this point, even if the grounds of appeal on this point were omitted from the lower judgment, it could not be said to have affected the judgment. In the end, this argument is without merit.

(3) 상관의 명령

Among the Grounds of Appeal, it is argued that the acts found by the lower court against Defendant D were acts in accordance with orders given by co-defendant A as Director of the Central Intelligence Agency and thus constitute lawful acts under Article 20 of the Criminal Act. We consider this argument.

Upon review, a public official, in performing duties, is under no authority by a superior to order a subordinate to commit a criminal act or other unlawful act. Also, while a subordinate has a duty to obey lawful orders from a superior within the organization, when the order is clearly unlawful or illegal, it cannot be regarded as an official directive order, and therefore there is no duty to follow it. Accordingly, this argument is plainly without merit.

2. 정당방위

Among the Grounds of Appeal, when the so-called “Busan-Masan incident” arose as a national resistance against the denial and infringement of popular sovereignty under the Yushin Constitution and emergency measures, and while the authorities were attempting to respond with indiscriminate massacre of the people, the Defendants reached the offense in this case as a last resort to defend the present unlawful infringement upon the lives and property of the sovereign people. It is argued that this constitutes self-defense and thus lacks unlawfulness; moreover, Defendant A had advanced such an explanation from the investigative authorities through the conclusion of the lower proceedings, but the lower court failed to fully hear this point or omitted to decide it. We consider this argument.

As repeatedly stated above, Defendant A’s act in this case, namely the murder with insurrectionary purpose and attempted insurrectionary leadership committed to kill the President and seize power through insurrection, has no obstacle to formation. Nevertheless, the Defendant argues that, based on the date of the offense, within a few days a popular uprising such as the so-called “Busan-Masan incident” would occur in Seoul, and that President Park would have ordered firing upon the people, so he committed this act because he intended to save the likely sacrificed lives, bodies, and property of the people, that is, to defend against the present unlawful infringement upon the legal interests of the people and the State.

However, according to the record, on October 19, 1979, the Defendant who had visited the scene and returned as the then Director of the Central Intelligence Agency on October 17 and 18, 1979, when asked at the first-instance trial whether there were any people who died in the Busan-Masan incident, answered that as far as he knew there were none.

Then even if expansion of the so-called Busan-Masan incident were anticipated, one could not conclude that not only injury to body or destruction of property but also necessarily the sacrifice of many lives would occur. Moreover, the allegation of the expansion of the Busan-Masan incident and of the President’s alleged order to fire is merely the Defendant’s own assertion, and there is no objective material supporting it. In this case, such an explanation is ultimately either fabricated falsehood by the Defendant or merely a fanciful inference about an uncertain future situation. Therefore, there is no evidentiary material establishing facts that satisfy the requirements for self-defense under Article 21(1) of the Criminal Act. Hence, the argument that the lower court overlooked this point lacks merit, and even if further hearing were conducted on this point, the possibility of obtaining materials to support it is slim in this case, so it cannot be said that there was a failure of hearing. Moreover, since no such illegality by the lower court exists, even if the lower judgment omitted consideration of this point, it could not be an illegality affecting the judgment. Accordingly, all of the above arguments are without merit.

3. 긴급피난

(1) Among the Grounds of Appeal, as in the domestic political situation at the time of October 26 noted in the above self-defense argument, Defendant A reached the offense in this case unavoidably to avoid the existing danger to the life, body, and freedom of numerous people. This constitutes necessity and thus lacks unlawfulness. Nevertheless, it is argued that the lower court overlooked this point and also failed to fully hear the argument, and further committed an illegality by omitting its determination. We consider this argument.

Upon review, for the same reasons already stated in the section on self-defense above, it is clear that this argument also lacks merit.

(2) Among the Grounds of Appeal, Defendant C maintained security, prohibited troop movement to the Blue House, and recommended declaration of martial law because he feared that if the fact that the head of state had been lost were leaked externally, it would lead to bloodshed from a gun battle among our own troops and give the North Korean regime an opportunity to provoke an invasion. Accordingly, these acts were unavoidable to avoid the present danger to the lives of many people and military/police personnel, and thus constitute necessity. Nevertheless, it is argued that the lower court overlooked this, misunderstood the law regarding necessity, and also omitted its determination despite Defendant C consistently maintaining this explanation in the first instance and appellate court, thereby committing a defect for lack of reasons. We consider this argument.

As noted in another section above, this Court has already held that the lower court’s measure recognizing Defendant C’s above conduct as constituting attempted major participation in insurrection is proper. This argument, even if those acts constitute the acts found in the lower judgment and the offense of major participation in insurrection, contends that they are exempt from unlawfulness because they were acts to avoid present danger to the lives of many people and military/police personnel caused by bloodshed from mutual gunfire among our own troops and the opportunity for the North to provoke an invasion.

Therefore, we examine whether Defendant C at that time truly had the intent to avoid such danger, that is, the intent of necessity. Looking at the record, it is evident that Defendant C had no true necessity intent. The later transfer of the President’s remains, the false report, and the concealment of the assassination show that participation in A’s insurrection came before any claimed desire to avoid danger. Thus the argument of necessity fails.

Section 8. 책임저각사유

Among the Grounds of Appeal, because Central Intelligence Agency personnel were in a more rigid superior-subordinate relationship than an army, with the Director at the apex, they had no room to determine whether a superior’s order was unlawful or to choose whether to execute it. Accordingly, Defendants D, E, F, G, and H, who acted in special circumstances where they could not refuse their superior’s orders, are said to have engaged in compelled acts or acts where no reasonable alternative existed, and thus cannot be punished.
