Nevertheless, it is argued that the lower court misunderstood the law concerning compelled acts and the absence of reasonable alternatives, thereby overlooking these grounds negating criminal responsibility. We consider this argument.

Upon review, the first instance held that public officials, in performing duties, are obligated to obey their immediate superior’s official orders, but are not obligated to obey clearly unlawful orders. Also, although it may be an unwritten rule among Central Intelligence Agency personnel that they must absolutely obey superior orders, that alone cannot make the clearly and flagrantly unlawful acts constituting the offenses found in this case into compelled acts or acts where lawful conduct cannot be expected. There is no other material showing that, at the time of the offense, the Defendants were unable to make free decisions because they were subjected to force that could not be resisted or threats that could not be prevented, nor that they were under special circumstances in which they could not refuse an unlawful order from a superior and thus lawful conduct could not reasonably be expected. Reviewing the record, it is easy to recognize that in light of the time and place of the offense, if the above Defendants had not been motivated by the desire for the so-called share they expected to receive in return for participating in this revolutionary act, they would have had enough time and spatial environment to refuse the superior’s order and escape from the scene. Thus the lower court’s judgment is all the more proper. Therefore, this argument lacks merit.

Section 9. 양형부당

Among the Grounds of Appeal, Article 432 of the Military Court-Martial Act provides that improper severity of sentence may be raised as a ground of appeal. However, since that article conflicts with Article 8 of the Constitution guaranteeing human dignity and Article 9 of the Constitution concerning equality of the people, in conjunction with Article 383 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and is therefore void, the Defendants sentenced to the death penalty should be allowed to appeal on the ground of improper severity of sentence. Considering the motive and purpose of the Defendants’ offenses in this case, the domestic political situation before and after the offenses, and their personal circumstances, as well as the fact that in more modern civilized countries many have already abolished the death penalty as punishment, and even theoretically the view favoring abolition is far superior, it is argued that the lower court’s imposition of the death penalty was excessively severe and thus improper. We consider this argument.

Upon review, military courts are special courts established for special purposes and objectives, unlike ordinary courts. Even if there is inequality between their treatment of defendants and that of ordinary courts, this is understood to have been anticipated by the Constitution and laws from the outset. Therefore, Article 432 of the Military Court-Martial Act cannot be regarded as an unconstitutional provision violating Articles 8 and 9 of the Constitution. Accordingly, the argument developed on the premise of such unconstitutionality lacks merit. However, on this point, Justices Min Mun-gi and Im Hang-jun have separate opinions.

Section 10. Conclusion

As seen above, there are separate opinions by (i) Justices Min Mun-gi, Yang Byeong-ho, Im Hang-jun, and Kim Yun-haeng as to part of Defendant A’s grounds of appeal; (ii) Justices Min Mun-gi, Yang Byeong-ho, Im Hang-jun, Kim Yun-haeng, and Seo Yun-hong as to part of Defendant C’s grounds of appeal; (iii) Justices Min Mun-gi, Yang Byeong-ho, Im Hang-jun, and Kim Yun-haeng as to part of Defendant D’s grounds of appeal; and (iv) Justices Min Mun-gi, Yang Byeong-ho, Im Hang-jun, Kim Yun-haeng, Jeong Tae-won, and Seo Yun-hong as to part of Defendants E, F, and G’s grounds of appeal. Nevertheless, according to the majority opinion, those grounds of appeal are without merit, and as to the other grounds of appeal, all participating Justices are unanimous that they lack merit. Accordingly, all appeals by the Defendants are dismissed. Also, in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices, as to Defendant H, pursuant to Article 57 of the Criminal Act, all days of pretrial detention in the appellate instance before this judgment is pronounced shall be credited against the principal sentence, and judgment is rendered as stated in the operative part.

Section 11. Separate opinions

1. Opinion of Supreme Court Justice Min Mun-gi

I consider the grounds of appeal submitted by counsel alleging an error of law concerning the legal principles of insurrection.

The insurrection at issue in this case is inherently a crime with a strong political coloration, and in reality it is accompanied by regime change, so a view of the political situation cannot be avoided.

As declared by the acting President AO, who succeeded the President who became vacant due to the offense of this case (October 26, 1979), through the confirmation declaration (November 10, 1979), the creation of a new constitution as a nationwide consensus is a milestone historical fact, a significant political decision of the people having undeniable prospectivity, an unwritten rule supported by the people’s legal conviction, and a binding force governing the political situation. However, because this consensus conflicts with the Yushin system and constitutes its true nature, it is clearly impossible without going beyond that system. Therefore, the very existence of nationwide consensus practically means the abolition of the Yushin system itself, and because this consensus cannot be said to have been achieved simultaneously with the fate of former President B, the Yushin system becomes, in legal logic, a system that shared the fate of the late President Park.

To help understanding, by way of example: if, in transforming the democratic order into a monarchical system, one were charged with insurrection, but a nationwide consensus was reached to change the Constitution into a monarchical constitution, then one could not punish the act as insurrection as it is. Since that consensus means the abolition of the democratic system, after the consensus, insurrection cannot mean a demand for democracy and certainly cannot mean a demand for monarchy; thus, one may not convict as insurrection merely because after consensus one seeks monarchy. The reason is that the protected legal interest differs because the constitutive basis differs, so the systems can no longer be regarded as the same as the constitutional order.

This case is exactly the same as that example, so the same legal principle applies.

Given the appellate judgment’s application of Article 87(1) and (2), Article 89, and Article 88 of the Criminal Act to all Defendants, and the purport explained as the reason, it is clear that all were treated as crimes with the purpose of subverting the Constitution. Moreover, according to Defendant A’s statements, which the lower court recognized as the leader, the purpose of the offense, as expressed, was to remove former President Park, the core of the Yushin system, terminate that system, and restore the democratic system. This cannot be denied on the record, and it is consistent with the original explanation. If one follows the lower judgment’s findings, the appellate court found that the Defendants killed the President and others as described in the judgment with the purpose of forcibly transforming the Yushin system, and considering the course of the litigation, it is clear that the trial was conducted after a nationwide consensus to amend the Constitution had already formed. Therefore, in this situation, because the basis of the act at the time of the offense and the basis at the time of trial are different, as explained above, this is a political situation that cannot be punished supra-legally. Thus, apart from whether the offense should be viewed as another crime, it cannot be punished as insurrection.

Accordingly, the lower judgment left a legal error affecting the conclusion, and the attempted-opinion supporting it is the same.

For the foregoing reasons, the argument is well-founded in conclusion, and I do not proceed to other claims.

Finally, in the alternative, I state my agreement with and incorporation by reference of the opinions of Justices Yang Byeong-ho, Im Hang-jun, and Kim Yun-haeng.

2. Opinion of Supreme Court Justice Yang Byeong-ho

I consider together the first, second, and third points of the appeal by Defendant A’s counsel I, the appeal grounds of AB, and the appeal grounds of AP for 17 persons.

According to the reasons in the lower judgment, Defendant A, while serving as Director of the Central Intelligence Agency, saw his plans to stabilize the political situation, which he himself drafted and implemented, repeatedly fail, exposing his incompetence in performance of duties, and after being reprimanded by President B, rumors of dismissal for responsibility circulated, making him feel insecure in his position. Meanwhile, although the President disliked the arrogant and overreaching attitude and interference by Chief T of the Presidential Security Service, who was his junior officer, he resented the President’s greater trust in T. From around an unknown date in April 1979, he planned to kill the President and seize power, independently devised the concrete plan for the act to maintain secrecy, chose the appropriate time, and decided to kill the President and others. After assassinating the President, he would declare martial law on the ground of national security and disturbance of public order, and using the authority and organizational force of the Central Intelligence Agency, take control of the martial law forces and suppress the situation by force, form a revolutionary committee overseeing legislative, judicial, and executive powers, become chairman himself and secure a base of power, and then run for President. The lower court recognized the facts of murder with insurrectionary purpose by finding that from 19:40 to around 20:05 on October 26, 1979, as found in the judgment, the President and others were shot to death.

However, in determining whether Defendant killed the President for the purpose of subverting the Constitution, reviewing the evidence the lower court adopted and considered in support of the insurrectionary-murder facts, the only relevant materials are the statements of the Defendant and co-defendant C in the first-instance and appellate military court, and the statements in the suspect-interrogation records prepared by the military prosecutor for the Defendant and C. Among them, Defendant’s statements in the first-instance and appellate court and the statements in the suspect-interrogation records prepared by the prosecutor indicate that this act of October 26 was done to abolish the undemocratic Yushin system for the lifetime rule of President B and to restore liberal democracy, the founding ideology and national policy. In view of the President’s strong desire to remain in power and his character of never retreating, the Defendant says that in this desperate situation there was no way to prevent this tragedy, so he was compelled to kill and remove the person because the restoration of liberal democracy and the sacrifice of the President’s life were fatefully connected. At the same time, he calls this act a revolution, saying that it was to eliminate the Yushin order, and that the revolutionary task was to declare martial law first to restore the situation, form a revolutionary committee and carry it out according to the basic organization and constitutional procedures, and that he intended to amend the Constitution through proper constitutional revision procedures.

In short, he says that he killed natural person B, the President, for the restoration of democracy, and that the other steps were to be taken through proper and lawful procedures. On this basis, the Defendant’s above statement is examined as a confession and the evidence for corroboration is scrutinized. However, on the crucial point of whether the purpose was truly to subvert the Constitution, the record does not supply adequate corroboration beyond abstract revolutionary language. The words “혁명,” “계엄선포,” and “혁명위원회” are too vague to equal a purpose of subverting the Constitution, especially in light of the fact that the same records also mention constitutional drafting, referendum, and elections under a new constitution. Thus, the lower judgment’s inference is too broad.

In this situation, the lower court, without considering these several points, conclusively held that the Defendant committed murder with insurrectionary purpose. This amounts either to a case of factual error without evidence or in violation of the rules of evidence, and in this case, where the crucial issue is whether it was merely the killing of a natural person holding the office of President or whether it was a murder with purpose of subverting the Constitution, the court should at least have further examined the facts and evidence. Failing to do so and broadly finding the facts amounts to a failure of hearing and defect for lack of reasons. Since that affects the judgment, the grounds of appeal are meritorious.

I consider together the grounds of appeal points 1, 2, 3, 4, and 6 submitted by Defendant C’s counsel AC, point 2 of the grounds of appeal by J Kim Hong-jae, and point 1 of the grounds of appeal by L.

According to the reasons in the lower judgment, Defendant C was appointed Chief Secretary to the President, and had long expressed dissatisfaction together with A regarding T’s arrogant and overreaching attitude and interference in authority, and had shown an intent to remove T. Then, on the day in question at around 17:50, when he arrived at the Central Intelligence Agency’s Gungjeong-dong restaurant to receive the President and sat with A on the curb in the garden in front of the restaurant entrance, during conversation he vented complaints such as saying, “That chief T fellow is so hard-line and troublesome,” and received from A the suggestion “Shall we get rid of that fellow today,” while recognizing that it meant killing T as the explosion of long-accumulated feelings, and consented thereto, thereby conspiring with A to kill T. Thereafter, although A repeatedly left the banquet table and even went outside for 15 minutes and came back, showing that the time for execution of the offense was imminent, he tolerated it; then at around 19:40 that same day, as a signal A lightly struck him with his right hand while saying, “Please take care of the President,” and fired a pistol at T. To facilitate the offense, Defendant C left the scene, thereby jointly with A killing T.

However, even if one carefully examines the evidence the lower court adopted, there is not the slightest trace of material supporting the conclusion that the Defendant and A conspired by communicating intent to kill Security Chief T of the President. The phrase “get rid of” cannot, in the context of these officials, be lightly construed as meaning “kill,” and the short exchange in the garden while waiting for the President’s arrival cannot reasonably be treated as a conspiracy to murder. The record shows, rather, that Defendant A had already firmly resolved to kill before meeting C, and that C’s reaction at most reflected vague assent or passivity, not a high-level plot necessary for conspiracy co-principal liability. Therefore, the lower court’s finding of co-principal liability is a grave error without evidence and a misunderstanding of law.

I consider together points 9 and 11 of the grounds of appeal by Defendant C’s counsel AC and point 2 of the grounds of appeal by L.

According to the reasons in the lower judgment, on the same day at around 19:43, Defendant C heard A say in front of the restaurant entrance, “It’s all over now. Please keep security tight,” and, as the only high-ranking state official to have witnessed A’s killing of the President, knowing that the security maintenance was an important mission that would determine the direction of the constitutional order in view of the influence attached to his position, he replied, “I understand,” agreeing to perform that duty according to the leader A’s order to maintain security. Thereafter, in order to maintain security for the offense and to use it later if the situation turned adverse as a pretext that he himself had tried to save the President, at around 19:55 that day he transported the President’s remains to the Seoul District Army Hospital and had the duty military doctor diagnose them, confirmed that “death had occurred five minutes earlier,” yet concealed the fact that the patient was the President and went to the Blue House Presidential Chief Secretary’s office, where he told the summoned chief secretaries and the Deputy Director of the Presidential Security Service, Army Lieutenant General AN, that “something has happened to the President and the chief T cannot now direct the troops, so strengthen the guard and closely control any rash actions; troop deployment from the Security Service is unnecessary.” Thereby he gained time to achieve the offense. At around 20:50, when he arrived there, he also told Prime Minister AO, who was then present, that “in the banquet hall, A and T fought and, in the end, the President died from a shot accidentally fired by A,” falsely reporting that A had intentionally killed the President. When asked by Ministers of Home Affairs and Justice AU and AV, he merely answered that “the President was injured,” thereby continuing to conceal A’s killing of the President. At around 21:10, after again receiving a telephone call from A ordering him to bring the Prime Minister, he went with the Prime Minister and the Ministers of Home Affairs and Justice to the Army Chief of Staff’s office in the Army Headquarters banka at around 21:30, saw A and then Minister of National Defense AW and major generals gathered there, and thought A had already taken control of the military. He then lied to the Minister of National Defense and others, saying, “The President has become absent; the incident happened because Chief T was too hard-line,” and proposed that they should bring the Prime Minister and restore order, thus inducing the declaration of martial law. At around 22:40, when in the Minister of National Defense’s office A, seated with the Prime Minister and other cabinet ministers, emphasized security maintenance and, in declaring emergency martial law, proposed that the reason should not be the President’s death but rather domestic security problems, Defendant C supported this and proposed as a compromise that martial law be declared on the ground of the President’s absence. At around 23:30, when the Prime Minister and the Ministers of Home Affairs and Justice showed no sign of agreeing with A and Blue House chief secretary Z urged him to explain the circumstances of the President’s absence at the cabinet meeting, Defendant concluded that A’s assertion would not be adopted, changed his attitude, and at around 00:30 the next day told the Minister of National Defense and the Army Chief of Staff that “A is the person who killed the President,” causing A to be arrested; thus the insurrectionary riot for the purpose of subverting the Constitution was not completed and the matter remained an attempt, which the lower court recognized as attempted major participation in insurrection.

However, the facts found by the lower court mean that after A killed the President in the restaurant and came out of the entrance asking Defendant to keep security tight and take care of the aftermath, the court found Defendant’s later conduct to constitute attempted major participation in insurrection. Yet the riot ended with the killing and the ensuing events were not themselves a riot that continued until arrest. Defendant’s later conduct involved some concealment and false reporting, but the evidence does not show that he was part of a continuing riot or that his acts were conspiratorial participation in such riot. Accordingly, the finding of attempted major participation in insurrection is unsupported.

I consider together point 1 of the grounds of appeal by Defendant D’s counsel N, point 3 of the grounds of appeal by counsel O for Defendants E and F, and point 3 of the grounds of appeal by counsel P for Defendant G.

According to the reasons in the lower judgment, at around 19:00 on the day of the incident, when Defendant A left the banquet table with the President and T in the restaurant and put one pistol prepared in advance in the second-floor bedroom of the main office into his pants watch pocket and was entering the banquet table, at around 19:10 in the old building garden adjacent to the restaurant he instructed Defendant D and first-instance defendant Park Heung-ju, saying, “I will take care of it today, so be prepared. I will handle the President and others directly, so as soon as you hear gunshots, pick three smart men and deal with the security guards,” and informed them that the Army Chief of Staff and the second assistant director were in the office, thereby urging them to solidify their will to participate in the offense, and received a promise from Defendant D that he would finish preparations within 30 minutes. Then, at around 19:15 in the west garden of the restaurant, Bureau Chief Kim Sun-ho instructed Defendants F and E, saying, “This is an order from the chief. If things go well today, you will get a share. When the chief fires from inside, shoot the security guards in the kitchen,” and received their assent. Defendant C, in the guard waiting room opposite the restaurant, received from Defendant D instructions to shoot the security guards if they came from the Blue House, and also, at around 20:05, received from Defendant E instructions to fire a confirmation shot at persons in the restaurant who were not yet fully dead. Defendant C then entered the security guards’ waiting room inside the restaurant, saw the guards being shot, recognized that this was a state of national upheaval, and agreed to participate according to the instruction. Thus each Defendant sequentially conspired to participate in killings for the purpose of subverting the Constitution. According to the same conspiracy, when at around 19:40 the sound of Defendant A’s pistol shot was heard as a signal, Defendant D fired his pistol toward the security guards in the waiting room in front of the restaurant entrance; Defendants E and F, together with Park Heung-ju, fired their pistols toward the President’s driver and security guards in the kitchen of the restaurant; and Defendant G, at around 20:05, carrying an M16 rifle, fired at the security guards lying in the restaurant waiting room and kitchen, as well as T groaning in the banquet table, thereby Defendant D, E, F, and G also jointly with Defendant A killed the President and others for the purpose of subverting the Constitution.

However, even if one carefully examines the evidence adopted by the lower court against the record, the offense plan in this case, as mentioned in the lower judgment, was independently devised by Defendant A for security reasons, and the words “I will take care of it today” said to Defendant D and first-instance defendant Park Heung-ju were first spoken to those two persons at around 19:10 that day. If at that time A gave the instruction that “I will take care of the President and others directly, so as soon as gunshots are heard, you take care of the security guards,” the natural meaning would be that they should cooperate in killing the President and others. Even if Defendant D knew that killing the President would bring about state upheaval, in this case there is no record showing any other particular instruction regarding the purpose of the act or other matters. Therefore, it would be a leap of logic inconsistent with our experience and logic to conclude that the Defendants participated in and carried out a killing of natural person B, the President, rather than a killing for the purpose of subverting the constitutional organ itself, the President, by force or making the exercise of its powers impossible. Even if Defendant D knew that the Army Chief of Staff and the second assistant director of the Central Intelligence Agency were in the main office at the time, that alone cannot change the conclusion.

Defendants E and F were those who received from Defendant D the instruction to shoot the security guards in the kitchen when gunshots are heard, and Defendant D said, “If today goes well, you will get a share.” However, those words were not spoken by A but were an independent remark by Defendant D. Even if the restaurant guards or drivers, no more than that, thought that getting a share would mean advancement or something major, and even if they knew that the Army Chief of Staff and the second assistant director of the Central Intelligence Agency were present, or even thought that this was a coup d’état bringing about upheaval against the State, that would merely reflect the Defendants’ awareness or thoughts in a system in which they blindly obeyed a superior’s directive. There is no basis for recognizing that “coup d’état” means the purpose of subverting the Constitution here, and such thoughts alone cannot constitute evidence of mutual conspiracy.

Defendant G, further down the chain, was the one who received from E the instruction to perform a confirmation killing on persons in the restaurant who had not yet died. It is shown that he did not think a state upheaval had occurred at the time, and he denies having ever muttered to himself that the die is cast, and there is no evidentiary material to the contrary.

Accordingly, not only Defendant G, but also Defendants E and F and Defendant D are properly viewed as unrelated to murderous acts for the purpose of subverting the Constitution. Yet the lower court recognized all of those Defendants as co-principals in murder with the purpose of subverting the Constitution. This cannot be denied to be a factual error without evidence or in violation of the rules of evidence, and this affected the judgment. Therefore, the grounds of appeal are meritorious.

3. Opinion of Supreme Court Justice Im Hang-jun

According to the appellate judgment, the lower court held that the acts of the Defendants other than Defendant C H corresponded to both the crime of murder with insurrectionary purpose under Article 88 of the Criminal Act and the crime of attempted insurrection under Article 87 of the Criminal Act, and that the two offenses are in imaginary concurrence; and it held that Defendant C’s acts corresponded to both murder and attempted insurrection. However, the lower court’s above holdings contain the following unlawful grounds: in this case the Defendants cannot be regarded as a combination of a number of persons sufficient to constitute a riot under Article 87, and therefore cannot be subjects of the crime of insurrection; even if viewed as such a combination, the acts correspond only to murder with insurrectionary purpose and cannot also be punished under Article 87 by imaginary concurrence; there is insufficient evidence to hold that the criminal acts of Defendants E, F, and C were murder with insurrectionary purpose; and there is no evidence to hold that Defendant C was a conspiracy co-principal in the killing of T with Defendant A.

I will set forth the reasons as follows. Article 87 of the Criminal Act provides that a person who riots for the purpose of usurping the territory or subverting the Constitution is punishable, and riot means a combination of many persons that through violence or intimidation disturbs the peace of a locality. Therefore, for the crime of insurrection to be established, a combination of many persons is indispensable. In this case, the number was too small to qualify as “many persons” in the legal sense, and the conduct did not satisfy the riot requirement. Even if the Defendants’ acts were a riot, once they committed murder, that conduct is absorbed into Article 88 and does not additionally become Article 87 by imaginary concurrence. Likewise, for Defendants E, F, and G, the evidence does not establish knowledge of the insurrectionary purpose, and for Defendant C there is no evidence of the high-level conspiracy required for conspiracy co-principal liability.

4. Opinion of Supreme Court Justice Kim Yun-haeng

Article 87 of the Criminal Act is the so-called collective offense of insurrection, and riot here means violence or intimidation by a combination of a mob sufficient to disturb the peace of a locality. In this case, taking the view that the acts of the Defendants do not constitute such a mob combination, I share the theory already expressed by Justice Im Hang-jun concerning that the six Defendants A, C, D, E, F, and G, excluding Defendant H, cannot be subject to the crime of insurrection, and also concerning that as to Defendant C, the lower judgment’s finding of conspiracy co-principal liability with A for the killing of T cannot be established.

Further, even if the insurrection offenses recognized by the lower court could apply to the Defendants, the lower court recognized as to the remaining Defendants other than Defendant C the relation of imaginary concurrence on the ground that their acts also corresponded to murder with insurrectionary purpose under Article 88. I point out that this legal application was mistaken because murder with insurrectionary purpose under Article 88 and riot in Article 87 are not to be duplicated in the way the lower court did. Thus the lower court’s sentencing framework is wrong.

5. Opinion of Supreme Court Justice Jeong Tae-won

This is the same as part (2) of the opinion of Supreme Court Justice Seo Yun-hong below concerning Defendants E and F, and part (3) concerning Defendant G.

6. Opinion of Supreme Court Justice Seo Yun-hong

In view of the facts and evidence in this case, I cannot agree with the majority opinion that would maintain the lower judgment finding all charges against Defendants C, E, F, and G guilty for the following reasons.

(1) As to Defendant C

First, regarding the offense of murder by conspiracy co-principal liability against this Defendant, the point of the lower court in finding this guilty is ultimately that the Defendant conspired with co-defendant A to kill the deceased T, the President’s security chief, and although he did not directly act, he caused A to carry out the killing and thus achieved the purpose. The supporting facts and evidence are summarized as follows: about two hours before the shooting, when the Defendant met A at the curb in the garden at the entrance to the Gungjeong-dong office, A said “I will get rid of the chief T,” and the Defendant nodded; he did not restrain A’s conduct at the shooting scene; and later that day, when the situation developed and Defendant met A in the restroom of the Army Headquarters banka and rebuked him, saying “Why did you even kill the President?”, from these things it was inferred that he intended the gunshot killing of T.

However, the so-called conspiracy co-principal liability is a concept concerning an execution principal. In light of social reality, in crimes by multiple persons there are cases where the substantive principal plans the crime behind the scenes and causes the execution act to be carried out by subordinates or persons under the principal’s control, and in such cases simple instigation or aiding and abetting is not enough. This theory emerged from judicial necessity. Even in such cases, the substantive principal must have the subjective intent to commit the crime as his own. Merely inducing another’s intent or tolerating or using another’s crime does not fall within this category. In this case, the lower court’s reasoning concerning Defendant C and the supporting facts are plainly not of that nature. The true subject of this shocking offense of assassinating the President was A, not Defendant C, and it is hard to understand that only with respect to the part of killing T the Defendant is treated as the principal and A as the executor under Defendant’s direction. Even if it is true that the Defendant nodded when A said “get rid of him,” that would, at most, mean he tolerated murder, and it is unclear why that can become a joint plot to kill. Likewise, even if he did not restrain A at the scene of the killing, that was merely passivity toward murder. More inexplicable still, the fact that the chief secretary Defendant did not restrain the shooting death of the President at the scene is not reproached in this case, yet failing to restrain the killing of the security chief is treated as conspiracy co-principal liability for murder. Also, the conversation in the Army banka restroom with A as a post hoc support for the plot is hard to accept when the plot itself is a major fact requiring strict proof.

Second, as to the attempted insurrection offense against the same Defendant, insurrection is a crime under Article 87 of the Criminal Act with the purpose of subverting the Constitution, and the concrete content of the Constitution at issue in this case is that the constitutional order was to be changed by assassinating the President. Therefore, whether Defendant had the intent to assassinate the President is indispensable for recognizing the purpose of insurrection against him.

However, at the time of filing the original indictment, it was stated as a factual allegation that Defendant also conspired with A to assassinate the President, but this part of the indictment was later amended in the lower court, and the lower court’s factual findings also finalized that Defendant had no relation to the assassination of the President. Therefore, attempted major participation in insurrection cannot be established against Defendant. The reporting after the assassination, and the later conduct, do not rise to the level of a proven participation in a riot for the purpose of subverting the Constitution. Thus the majority opinion cannot be followed.

(2) As to Defendants E and F

The lower judgment finding these Defendants guilty of attempted insurrection and murder with insurrectionary purpose also cannot be left standing. It is undeniable that, as co-defendants and subordinates of D, they shot and killed U and X, security guards of the Presidential Security Service, while staying at the Gungjeong-dong intelligence restaurant on the day of the offense. However, for that act to be murder with insurrectionary purpose, there must be awareness of the insurrectionary purpose, namely subversion of the Constitution. On this point, the only materials the lower court or the majority opinion regarded as evidence are the statements the Defendants made during the military investigation. Their statements merely amount to saying they thought that if things went well, they would be promoted or get a share. To say that those statement entries are sufficient evidence that they knew of subversion of the Constitution, i.e. the assassination of the President, and participated in the offense exceeds the bounds of free conviction.

As to how those statements were made, the record shows they were the result of leading questions and inferences made by the military investigative authorities, so one cannot distinguish whether they are opinions or statements of fact. It is hard to understand how they can be linked to awareness of the assassination of the President or subversion of the Constitution. Regarding the circumstances by which the Defendants came to shoot, co-defendant D merely instructed them to drive the security guards in the restaurant into a corner and, if they resist, return fire. Defendant F was D’s driver, and E was also a guard at Gungjeong-dong with little education. Even if one has difficulty asking them about the meaning of subverting the Constitution, the minimum would be awareness of the assassination of the President. Yet there is no clear material in this case showing even that awareness on their part. To uphold a death sentence by recognizing that all of this existed is unacceptable.

(3) As to Defendant G

This Defendant is recognized by the lower court as having committed attempted insurrection and murder with insurrectionary purpose by carrying out so-called confirmation killing 30 minutes after the gunfire in this case, thereby completely extinguishing the lives of T and U, who were still alive at the time. This part also cannot be left standing.

The time of the above confirmation killing by the Defendant is fixed by the lower court as 20:05 on that day, whereas the shooting of Chief T by A was at 19:40. Then it is difficult, in view of the various materials, to conclude that even 25 to 30 minutes after the first shot T was still groaning and had not died. On that day A shot T, then fired at the President, and shortly thereafter hid in the restroom, then fired the final shot into T’s abdomen and again shot the President; the record and the lower court both accept this. Then T’s time of death would have been at least before, or at the same time as, the President’s death. The hospital authorities stated that the President’s time of death was five minutes before the time the body was transported to the military hospital, that is, before 19:57 that day. In the end, if the President’s time of death can be estimated as 10 to 12 minutes after A’s first shooting, then T’s time of death would also be 19:50 or 19:52. Then it would be reasonable to conclude that at the time of Defendant G’s confirmation killing at 20:05, the victim T had already died. Otherwise, because the autopsy report and photographs of the body are in the record and the exact location of the gunshot wounds is clearly shown, the court should have had an expert assess the time of death and conducted a hearing accordingly.

Nevertheless, without taking such measures, to recognize murder with insurrectionary purpose and even impose the death penalty merely on the Defendant’s statement that T seemed to be making some sound at the time of the confirmation killing is utterly incomprehensible. Therefore, failing to examine this point and determine whether it was murder or merely a gunshot at a corpse amounts to a failure of hearing or defect for lack of reasons. Moreover, the record does not show where or what the Defendant was doing before the confirmation killing. To recognize guilt for insurrection on the ground that the killing was for an insurrectionary purpose is also not free from the criticism of finding facts without evidence.

For these reasons, I cannot agree with the majority opinion that would maintain the Army High Military Court judgment on Defendants C, E, F, and G, and I state that the grounds of appeal on these points are meritorious.

In perjury, the false statement referred to does not mean that the objective fact is false, but means a statement made contrary to one’s memory of facts personally experienced, that is, 기억에 반하는 사실; and according to the record of this case, not only has the Defendant consistently denied criminal intent, but even according to the respective entries in the statement prepared by the judicial police officer concerning the complainant 이월분 and the written statement prepared by 이월분, the said 이월분 herself stated that, between her and the above 조보경, there were 거래관계 concerning a mutual-aid fund and the management of a teahouse, as well as 거래관계 concerning deposits, and that there was an occasion when she applied 165,200 won out of the deposits to the mutual-aid fund and deducted it, and gave the remaining 34,800 won to 조보경, however, she claimed that the deposit was 200,000 won, and thus, after deducting the above 165,200 won, the remainder was 34,800 won, so that there is a difference of 100,000 won each between the deposit and the payment. Although 이월분 denies the fact of running a teahouse as a partnership with 조보경, stating that she employed 조보경 as the teahouse madam, and denies having received 700,000 won as partnership funds, what this means is that, separate from such transactions, there was a deposit to be returned to 조보경, and that she returned the remaining money after deducting 165,200 won therefrom; accordingly, it cannot be concluded that the Defendant’s testimony, in light of the above facts, was a false statement contrary to memory, and no other evidence can be found sufficient to establish that the Defendant’s testimony was a false statement contrary to memory. Therefore, if the trier of fact was to recognize the Defendant’s criminal intent, it should first have further examined the various 거래관계 between the above 조보경 and 이월분 and determined whether the Defendant’s testimony was wholly implausible; nevertheless, without fully conducting such examination, it held that testimony which substantially accorded even with the objective facts asserted by 이월분 was a false statement, and thus it is deemed to have erred by misunderstanding the legal principle of the offense of perjury, by failing to conduct sufficient examination, and by violating the rules of evidence and misapprehending the facts.
